Reviewing a Saved Health Snapshot

When Health Monitor data is included in Log Collection, SAT writes a human-readable file named <HOSTNAME>-SystemHealth.txt. The file contains a versioned SAT health-data section that Health Monitor can load later.

To load a saved Health Monitor snapshot on the engineer workstation, do the following:
  1. Download the customer-provided collection from the normal case portal.
  2. If the collection is a ZIP archive, extract the <HOSTNAME>-SystemHealth.txt file.
  3. Start SAT in Engineer Review Workstation mode.
  4. Open Health Monitor.
  5. Select Load saved snapshot....
  6. Select the <HOSTNAME>-SystemHealth.txt file.
  7. Confirm that Health Monitor displays SAVED SNAPSHOT with the original machine and capture time.
  8. Review the health details or add relevant Health Monitor rows to the active case note.
Result. The engineer can review the captured system state without running live diagnostics on the engineer workstation.

Tools > Tools Overview

Tools Overview

Tools holds the checks that run on this machine, by category. Run them in the Customer / Lab role. The tiles at the top are the categories, each with how many tools it holds; a tile opens its category's page, where its own tile shows pressed in. The Tools page itself lists every category with its tools beneath its name. In the sidebar, the arrow beside Tools opens and closes the list of categories.

CategoryTools
Log CollectionUniversal Veeam Log Collection, Custom Paths
Guided DiagnosticsScenarios by symptom; the scenarios that fit the products and roles found on this machine
Network ToolsRemote Port Checker, Local Port Checker, Name Check, File Transfer Calculator, TLS Handshake, Windows RPC Connectivity, gRPC Connectivity, Veeam Service Channel, SMB Connectivity, TCP / UDP Listener, Local Loopback Self-Test, gRPC Listener, Packet Capture, Network Throughput
SQL ToolsPermission check, Server shape, Backups and log chain, Database files, Read-only query
VSS ToolsEnumerate VSS Writers, Run VSS Test Job
System DifferencesFile Differences, Registry Differences
WMI DiagnosticsWMI Health, WMI Cluster Diagnostics, Custom WMI Query
VBR DiagnosticsRunning VBR Jobs; shown on a backup server
Host DiagnosticsTime Check, File Lock Check, Volume Check, Service and Process Watch, Host Checks, Process Inventory, Named Pipes, Installer Cache Check

Last Tool Output is a tile that appears after a tool has run in this session. Its cards prepare that run's output, with its hostname, manifest and SHA-256 hashes, for transfer to the review workstation, and delete it once it has been transferred.

Before a tool runs

Each tool opens on a card where its results will be: what it does, then OPTIONS with a line for each field and check box shown, whether it is Required or Optional, what it does, and the button that runs it. Press F1 for that tool's own article. A Guided Diagnostics scenario's card also lists the machine to run it on and what to set up first (SETUP); for the other tools, what to prepare is in the tool's article in this guide, under Before you start. The card gives way to the results when the tool starts, and returns after Reset Output.

Fields that offer values

A field with a known set of values offers them: its Browse button reads Choose... and opens them in a menu. The value picked goes into the field, and anything typed is still taken. Port fields offer Veeam's ports by number with the role that uses each; Hash mode, Ambiguous date order, Assumed UTC offset minutes and WMI namespace offer theirs.

A long run's progress

Log Review and Log Collection list their progress as they go: a row for each file or step reached, the one in hand marked Current and each before it Done, with the count (3 / 20) in its own column. The run's results replace the list when it ends.

On Customer / Lab, each run keeps its output beside SAT until it is prepared or deleted. See Last Tool Output.

To run a tool, do the following:
  1. Switch to the Customer / Lab role. The categories are listed under Tools in the rail, and Go > Tools opens the Tools page.
  2. Choose a category tile, then the tool's card. A hint card opens first, with what the tool does and an OPTIONS line for each field and tick box.
  3. Fill the form and choose the tool's button, such as Test TCP or Run check.
  4. Read the table. After a run the form folds to give the result room; choose Edit to open it again. Select a row to read it in full in the pane under the table.
  5. Choose Show CLI to see the command that repeats the run on the command line.

A table sizes its columns to their contents, and the spare width goes to the widest column. A column you drag keeps its width until new rows arrive. A divider separates the table from the pane under it.

Open one with its key, from the Tools menu, from the QUICK TOOLS row on the Customer / Lab Home, from its card on Network Tools or Host Diagnostics, or with Jump To (Ctrl+K). The key brings an open window to the front. F1 in the window opens the tool's article in the Help window.

  • Copy gives the result as text. In Engineer Review, Add to #note keeps it with the active case.
  • On Customer / Lab each run keeps its result beside SAT as tool output (result.json, report.txt and result.tsv), so a log collection carries it. The newest run of Name Check, Time Check, Local Port Checker, Volume Check and File Lock Check shows under Quick checks in Environment Review. In Engineer Review those views show the runs a case's imported collections carry.
  • Each run is recorded in Recent Activity.
  • A few checks read more as administrator; each article says which.

Each tool has a command-line twin, listed under Quick checks in --help and in the CLI User Guide.

To open a quick tool, do the following:
  1. Press the tool's key: F2, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10 or F12. Or choose the tool in the Tools menu, in the QUICK TOOLS row of the Customer / Lab Home, or in Jump To.
  2. Use the tool in its window. Copy gives the result as text, and Add to #note keeps it with the active case in Engineer Review.
  3. Press the key again to bring the open window to the front. Press F1 in the window to read the tool's article.

Tools > Last Tool Output

Last Tool Output

Supported Customer/Lab tools write tool-named output below Log-Collections/Tools/<ToolName>. A run can contain result.tsv, retained diagnostic files, integrity information, and tool-state.txt. These files preserve the diagnostic result for collection, transfer, and later case review.

Tool output folders, cards, logs, and transfer views use the diagnostic name so collected evidence can be identified without opening the result file first.

Prepare Tool Output

The normal customer transfer path is Universal Log Collection, which recursively includes all current tool outputs under the bundle's Tools/ directory. Individual tool output can still be prepared when only that diagnostic is required.

Delete Last Local Tool Output

Manual delete is available when required. Customer/Lab support-bundle cleanup can remove safely archived transient output automatically; Engineer Review does not delete its application/case data through this mechanism.

Tools > Log Collection > Universal Veeam Log Collection

Universal Veeam Log Collection

Universal Log Collection gathers selected Veeam logs, Windows/Linux/macOS support context, environment.log, SAT Health/system evidence, and SAT tool output from the local customer/lab machine into one support ZIP.

Before you start

  • To include the output of diagnostic tools, run any tools whose results belong in the case first: the collection takes the output of the tools run on this machine.
  • For the full set, start SAT as administrator first. With administrator rights the collection also gathers VSS providers, shadow copies, shadow storage and writers, filesystem minifilters, boot configuration and Windows servicing packages. Without them it still runs, and the sections that could not be collected are recorded in the bundle. When SAT is not elevated, it asks once whether to run the collection with administrator rights.
To collect the Veeam logs of the products found here, do the following:
  1. In Customer / Lab, open Tools > Log Collection and choose Universal Veeam Log Collection.
  2. Fill in the fields. The table below describes each.
  3. Choose Collect selected products.

Use Last X days to limit large Veeam/Event Log collections. Leave it blank to collect all eligible logs. The time filter is optional and is applied to eligible Veeam log files and Windows Event Log export.

Transferable tool output is stored below Log-Collections/Tools/<ToolName>. Persistent/operator application state such as debug/activity is stored separately under ApplicationLogs. The bundle copies tool output as Tools/ and application state as ApplicationLogs/.

Customer cleanup boundary. After a complete Customer/Lab ZIP succeeds, SAT removes successfully archived transient Tools/ApplicationLogs and the uncompressed staging directory. If staging is incomplete, collection is cancelled, or ZIP creation fails, originals are preserved. Engineer Review never performs whole-workspace cleanup.
FieldWhat it does
Last X days (optional; blank = ALL)Optional. Collects only logs and events from the last N days, a whole number. Empty collects all of them.
Output folderRequired. The folder the collected bundle is written to. It starts filled in, and an empty field is refused.
Create ZIP archiveOptional. Ticked, the collection is also written as one ZIP file, and the loose folder is removed once the ZIP is complete. Ticked to begin with.
Include sanitized third-party operational/error logs (SQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, etc.)Optional. Ticked, the operational and error logs of database products found on this machine are collected with sensitive values sanitized. Database contents are not collected. Ticked to begin with.

Tools > Log Collection > Selecting Detected Products

Selecting Detected Products

When Universal Log Collection opens, SAT builds a product list for the current operating system. Products strongly detected on the local machine are selected by default. Other products that can exist on that operating system may be shown unchecked for explicit engineer selection.

To review the collection product list, do the following:
  1. Open Tools > Log Collection > Universal Veeam Log Collection.
  2. Review the detected product names. SAT uses full product names, for example Veeam Backup & Replication, Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows, Veeam Agent for Linux, Veeam Agent for Mac, or an applicable Veeam plug-in.
  3. Leave the detected products selected unless that product's logs are intentionally outside the requested collection.
  4. Select another applicable product only when you know its evidence should be included but local detection could not establish it.
  5. Use Custom Paths for approved evidence outside the catalog paths.
Multiple products are normal. A VBR server can also contain a local Agent, plug-in, or management component. Selecting several products creates one host collection with deduplicated physical sources, not unrelated product ZIP files.

Tools > Log Collection > Supporting Third-Party Logs

Supporting Third-Party Logs

When enabled, SAT can collect a bounded set of operational/error logs from supporting applications that commonly participate in the observed Veeam workflow. This option is separate from Integrations, which manages optional diagnostic utilities.

Examples can include Microsoft SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Oracle, MySQL/MariaDB, or MongoDB operational/error logs where SAT has a defined safe source. Database data files, database dumps, repository payloads, customer documents and arbitrary application data are not collected because a database product is installed.

Redaction is best-effort, not a guarantee. SAT avoids known customer-data locations and redacts high-risk text patterns where practical. Review the collection manifest and transferred evidence according to the normal support-data handling process. See Privacy and Collection Boundaries.

Tools > Log Collection > System and Health Context

System and Health Context

Universal Log Collection captures equivalent classes of host diagnostics on Windows, Linux and macOS using each platform's native mechanisms.

PlatformSupporting context
WindowsOS/system/hardware, installed software, CBS/QFE hotfixes and DISM packages, service inventory/state, disks/sector context, VSS/minifilters, adapter/driver context, IPv4/IPv6 interface MTU/metrics, routes, advanced adapter properties, bound/listening connections, firewall/SCHANNEL/TLS cipher context, public Veeam-named certificate metadata, redacted read-only Veeam Registry inventory, selected Windows Event Logs, Health Monitor, Veeam product roles and SAT tool output.
LinuxOS/kernel/CPU/memory, uptime, filesystems/block devices, detailed links/MTU/addressing, routes and policy rules, listening ports/processes where available, services and service enablement, package inventory, OpenSSL/TLS cipher context, Health Monitor, Veeam roles and tool output.
macOSmacOS/kernel/hardware/memory, filesystems, interface/addressing, default route, listening network state, launch services, installed applications, Health Monitor, Veeam roles and tool output.

The bundle-root environment.log is a bounded portable snapshot of the most useful machine/product/network/service/software/security context. The current format is SAT_ENVIRONMENT_V2. Engineer Review loads it read-only and also accepts earlier SAT_ENVIRONMENT_V1 snapshots.

Structured tool output retains the diagnostic result, status, and integrity information required for case transfer and later review. Tool folders and result views use the diagnostic name.

Tools > Log Collection > Collecting on a Customer or Lab System

Collecting Logs on a Customer or Lab System

On the customer's or the lab's machine, Log Collection builds a support bundle of the Veeam logs to send back for review.

To create a transferable support bundle, do the following:
  1. Start SAT on the customer/lab host and use Customer/Lab role.
  2. Open Tools > Log Collection > Universal Veeam Log Collection.
  3. Review detected product checkboxes. Shared roots such as Veeam\Backup are collected as common evidence but do not make SAT claim VBR is installed.
  4. Optionally enter Last X days; blank means all eligible logs.
  5. Keep platform/system context enabled unless the case specifically excludes it.
  6. Run the collection and inspect any Warning/Error result row. Double-click a row without an openable source line to view the full recorded details.
  7. Verify the ZIP path and transfer that ZIP through the normal support process.
Result. The ZIP contains Veeam evidence, Tools, ApplicationLogs, platform support context and environment.log. Successful Customer/Lab archival removes the transient uncompressed SAT collection state that was safely included; failures preserve it for recovery.
Windows Event Logs. SAT uses the native Windows Event Log API to export selected channels. If Windows denies or fails an export, the collection records a warning/error with the native code.

Tools > Log Collection > Collecting Without a Case

Collecting Without a Case

A customer/lab collection does not require a case. In No Case, SAT keeps the collection portable and does not create case-owned parser/note data to gather logs.

Customer/Lab Recent Activity remains useful while work is running. When a bundle is generated, the current activity file is archived as <MACHINENAME>Activity.tsv. Engineer Review can open that collected file read-only without replacing or appending to the engineer workstation's live activity file.

After a Customer/Lab bundle completes, SAT removes the transient files it created on that machine: application logs, tool output and staging. They are already inside the bundle, so nothing is lost, and this is what lets SAT be carried onto a customer machine, run, and removed without leaving anything behind.

This only happens in the Customer/Lab role. In Engineer Review, the role your own workstation runs in, nothing is removed after a collection. Your workstation holds the case history, so a role that cleaned up after itself would take the activity trail with it. The role badge in the header tells you which one you are in; see Workspace Roles.

Related topics

Universal Veeam Log Collection
Tools > Log Collection > Privacy and Collection Boundaries

Privacy and Collection Boundaries

Environment security inventory: SAT reads public certificate metadata and selected diagnostic Registry/package/service/network state only. Private certificate keys are not collected. Windows Veeam Registry inventory is read-only and redacts values whose names indicate passwords, secrets, tokens, credentials, private keys, connection strings, access keys or authorization material.

SAT is designed to gather troubleshooting evidence, not arbitrary customer data. Automatic collection uses known product/system sources and bounded supporting logs, not entire user, database or repository trees.

Examples of data not collected automatically

  • Backup repository payloads and protected-file contents.
  • Database data files, database dumps, redo/archive payloads, WAL/archive sets, or customer query results.
  • Arbitrary home/profile directories.
  • All of /var/log or another large system log tree without a defined source.
  • Environment-variable dumps or process command lines that can contain credentials/tokens.
  • Private certificate keys.

Official Veeam exporters

Some Veeam products provide their own support export commands. SAT can invoke an approved exporter only when that option is explicitly selected. Vendor-generated output is isolated and identified because an official support bundle can legitimately contain broader configuration/system information than SAT's conservative automatic collector.

Supporting application logs

Third-party operational/error logs are limited to known diagnostic sources. SAT applies best-effort high-risk text redaction where defined, but no automated redaction process should be treated as a guarantee that every possible sensitive value has been removed.

Tools > Guided Diagnostics

Guided Diagnostics Overview

Guided Diagnostics starts from the problem: choose the scenario that matches the symptom, fill in what it asks for, and run it. Each step is one of SAT's read-only checks, in order. A step that decides the case stops the run when it fails; Keep going after a failure runs every step. Each step's row says what was found, what it means in Veeam's terms, what to do next, and the Veeam page or KB it follows. The Result row and the Case note rows below it are the block to paste into the case. Scenarios that do not apply to the products found here are not listed.

A scenario's card shows, before it runs, where to run it (RUN IT ON), what to prepare (SETUP), what each step checks and what the results mean, then its OPTIONS: each field with whether it is Required or Optional and what it does, and the Keep going after a failure box. The sections below give the same for each scenario.

ScenarioUse it whenSteps
Managed server cannot be reachedAdding or rescanning a server fails, or a managed server shows as unavailable.Name resolution; Clock difference; Ports for the role; Payload to a SAT listener; Windows RPC endpoint mapper; WMI on the server
Application-aware processing of SQL Server failsA job's guest processing of SQL Server fails or truncates no logs.SQL Server service; SQL Server VSS writer; Guest processing account rights; NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM fallback; SQL writer events
SQL transaction log backup fails or the chain is brokenLog backups fail, or a restore says the logs do not match a backup.Backups and the log chain; Availability groups and backup preference
Backup to repository is slowA job runs longer than expected; the statistics name a bottleneck.Bottleneck; Repository volume
Veeam Agent cannot connect to its backup serviceThe Agent's tray or control panel reports Failed to connect with the backup service.Service channel
Backup server cannot reach its configuration databaseThe Veeam Backup Service does not start, or the console cannot connect to the database.Configuration database; Database server reachable; Service account's rights on the database; PostgreSQL authentication
Snapshot (VSS) fails during backupA job fails at the snapshot, or a writer is reported as failed.VSS writers; Volume Shadow Copy service; VSS events
Certificate or TLS error between Veeam componentsA component reports a certificate, trust or TLS error when connecting.Name resolution; Clock difference; TLS handshake
RPC or port exhaustionA Veeam task, service or console fails with The RPC server is unavailable, Only one usage of each socket address, or a connection that cannot be made, and a process cannot open another socket or port.Dynamic port range and TIME_WAIT delay; Port exhaustion events; Ports in use against the range; Which process holds the ports; Handles and kernel pool; Pool exhaustion events; RPC services; RPC dynamic port restriction; Windows Firewall for RPC; RPC endpoint mapper on the other machine
To run a scenario, do the following:
  1. Open Tools > Guided Diagnostics in the Customer / Lab role and choose the card whose title matches the symptom.
  2. Fill the inputs. Each field has hover help, and the hint card above the form gives an OPTIONS line for each field and tick box.
  3. Tick Keep going after a failure to run every step and list each failure. Leave it clear to stop at the first step that decides the case.
  4. Choose Run scenario. Each step appears as a row with its status, what was found and what the status means.
  5. Select a row to read the whole step in the pane under the table.
  6. Select the CASE NOTE row at the end to read the note that is ready to copy into the case.

Where to run each scenario and what its steps check

Every step tests from the machine SAT runs on, so the machine matters: the same scenario run on another machine answers for that machine's view. Each scenario below names the machine to run it on, what to set up first and its options, then lists its steps with what each one reads or sends and what a result means in Veeam's terms.

Tools > Guided Diagnostics > Reading a result

Reading a result

Each step's row shows its status, what was found, and the scenario's own words for what that status means and what to do next. The table closes with a RESULT row, the verdict of the run, and a CASE NOTE row, ready to copy: select it to read the note in the pane under the table. A step that decides the case stops the run when it fails; the steps after it read Not run. Keep going after a failure runs every step and lists each failure, the first one first.

StatusMeaning
PassThe step found nothing wrong. The row says what was read.
AttentionThe step found something to look at. The run goes on, and the result counts it.
FailThe step found a problem. The row says what was found, what it means and what to do next.
Not applicableThe step does not apply here, such as a Windows step on Linux or a SQL Server that is another machine.
Could not checkThe step could not read what it needs, such as a server that does not answer or a right SAT lacks. The row says why.
Not runAn earlier step that decides the case failed, so the step was skipped.

Related topics

Guided Diagnostics Overview
Tools > Guided Diagnostics > Managed server cannot be reached

Managed server cannot be reached

Adding or rescanning a server fails, or a managed server shows as unavailable.

Before You Begin

Run it on. On the backup server, the machine that fails to reach the managed server. Every step tests from the machine SAT runs on toward the server named in the field, so the result is that machine's view of the path.

  • To run steps 1 to 3, note the managed server's name, role and operating system in the Veeam console first, on the backup server.
  • Optional: to compare the two clocks in step 2, make sure a time service on the managed server answers SNTP queries on UDP port 123 first, on the managed server. Without an answer step 2 reads Could not check and the other steps still run.
  • Optional: to run step 4, start a TCP listener on the managed server first. In SAT on the managed server open Tools > Network Tools, choose the TCP listener operation, set Listen port to the SAT listener port (2500 by default) and Duration seconds to 600, and choose Listen; leave it running until the scenario has finished. Tick Accept multiple connections until timeout to run the scenario again without restarting it. Without the listener, or when a firewall blocks its port, step 4 reads Could not check and the other steps still run.
  • Optional: to let step 4 reach the listener on a Windows managed server, allow SAT when Windows asks whether to allow it to listen on the network, first, on the managed server. The answer stays as a firewall rule. Without it Windows Firewall blocks inbound connections to the listener and step 4 reads Could not check.
  • To run step 6, start SAT first as an account that WMI on the managed server allows, usually an administrator of that server, on the backup server. The step connects to the server as the account running SAT, and without that access it fails.
To run the scenario, do the following:
  1. In Customer / Lab, open Tools > Guided Diagnostics and choose Managed server cannot be reached.
  2. Fill in the options. The table below describes each.
  3. Tick Keep going after a failure to run every step.
  4. Choose Run scenario.
  5. Copy the Result and Case note rows into the case note.
Expected result. Each step reads Pass, Attention, Fail, Not applicable, Could not check or Not run, with what it means and what to do next.

Options.

OptionWhat it does
Server name or addressRequired. The managed server every step tests from this machine, typed as the Veeam console lists it, or its IP address. Left empty, every step reads Could not check.
Server roleOptional. The server's role in Veeam, picked from the list. Step 3 tests the TCP ports the Veeam ports page lists for that role. Default agent-windows.
Server's systemOptional. Which system's ports step 3 tests, Windows or Linux. A role that lists ports for one system only, such as a backup repository (445 on Windows, 22 on Linux), needs it. Left empty, the system the role names is used (agent-windows or agent-linux); a role that lists ports for one system only and names none reads Could not check.
SAT listener portOptional. The port the SAT listener on the managed server listens on. Step 4 connects to it, so it has to match Listen port on the managed server. Default 2500.
VBR versionOptional. 12 or 13, the Veeam Backup & Replication version the server belongs to. Step 3 tests the ports that version's guide lists. Left empty, it tests the ports of VBR 12 and VBR 13 and names the version of each port only one of them lists.
Keep going after a failureOptional. Ticked, every step runs and each failure is listed. Cleared, the run stops at the first failure of a step marked as stopping the run, and the steps after it read Not run.
StepWhat it checksWhat the result means
1. Name resolutionLooks the name up the way this machine does: the hosts file first, then each DNS server this machine is configured with, asking each for the IPv4 and then the IPv6 addresses. The addresses in the row are the ones this machine's resolver returns, and the row says where the answer came from first. A typed IP address passes. The step fails when the resolver returns no address. A failure here stops the run.Fail. Veeam reaches managed servers by the name they were added with; it has to resolve from the backup server. Next: Correct the DNS record or the hosts entry, then rescan. Source: Ports (Veeam Backup & Replication 13 User Guide).
Attention. The hosts file has an entry for this name and a DNS server also answers for it, or the DNS servers answer with different addresses, so the name can lead to a machine other than the one intended. Next: Compare the addresses with the managed server's current address, then correct the hosts entry or the DNS record.
2. Clock differenceSends one SNTP request on UDP port 123 from this machine to the server, waits up to 3 seconds for the answer and compares the server's clock with this one. A difference over 1 minute needs attention and over 5 minutes fails. A server that does not answer SNTP reads Could not check.Fail. Kerberos refuses authentication when clocks differ by more than 5 minutes. Next: Correct the time source of the machine that is off.
Attention. The clocks differ by more than a minute. Kerberos refuses authentication when clocks differ by more than 5 minutes. Next: Correct the time source of the machine that is off.
3. Ports for the roleOpens a TCP connection from this machine to the server on each port in the chosen role's entry of the Veeam ports page, waits up to 3 seconds for an answer from each and closes it again; no data is sent. The entries are those for the server's system, Windows or Linux: the one chosen in Server's system, else the one the role names, as the page lists some ports for one system only. A range such as 6184 to 6195, where a service takes the first free port, passes when any port in it answers. A closed port the page marks optional needs attention, as the server may not use that feature; a closed required port fails. Ranges held only while a job or a failover uses them, such as 2500 to 3300, and the ports a server holds on the loopback address only are left out. A role that lists ports for one system only, with no system chosen and none named by the role, reads Could not check. A failure here stops the run.Fail. A port the Veeam page lists as required for this role did not accept a connection: it is closed, or a firewall drops the attempt. Closed optional ports are listed in the row separately. Next: Open the required ports end to end, in every firewall on the path, and check each closed optional port against the features in use. Source: Ports (Veeam Backup & Replication 13 User Guide), Veeam KB2065.
Attention. Only ports the Veeam page marks optional are closed. Each belongs to a feature the server may not use; the row names it. Next: Open a listed optional port only if the server uses its feature.
4. Payload to a SAT listenerOptional. Opens one TCP connection from this machine to the port in SAT listener port (2500 by default) on the server, waiting up to 3 seconds, and looks for a SAT listener there. When one answers, this machine sends 50 MiB generated in memory, and the listener answers with the byte count and SHA-256 it received; the step compares both with what was sent and gives the rate. Both machines hash the data in memory as it passes. A port that does not answer, or that answers and is not a SAT listener, reads Could not check, as the step needs the listener started on the server first; Set up first says how. A listener that answers and does not verify the payload fails the step.Fail. The SAT listener on the server answered, but the stream did not arrive intact: the connection broke during the transfer, or the byte count or SHA-256 differed. A firewall or inspection device that drops or alters long connections can do this, so can a listener stopped or closed during the transfer, and so can a path slower than about 7 Mbit/s, as the listener allows 60 seconds for the 50 MiB. Next: Start the listener again, leave it running and repeat the step. If it fails again, test the same path from each end with the Remote Port Checker and look at the devices between the two machines.
5. Windows RPC endpoint mapperConnects from this machine to TCP port 135 on the server and sends a DCE/RPC bind request to the RPC endpoint mapper, which a working RPC service answers with a bind acknowledgement. Each stage waits up to 5 seconds, and the row names the stage that failed, the connection or the bind. A server whose system is Linux, chosen in Server's system or named by its role, reads Not applicable. Only port 135 is tested; the dynamic ports RPC services use afterwards are outside this step. A failure here stops the run.Fail. Deployment with credentials and remote operations on a Windows server use RPC (135) and SMB (445). Next: Allow RPC and the dynamic RPC range, or use certificate-based deployment. Source: Ports (Veeam Backup & Replication 13 User Guide).
6. WMI on the serverRuns one WMI query on the server over DCOM, as the account running SAT: SELECT Caption, Version, CSName FROM Win32_OperatingSystem in the root\cimv2 namespace. The row gives the operating system and computer name it returned. The connection and the answer each wait up to two minutes. A server whose system is Linux, chosen in Server's system or named by its role, reads Not applicable.Fail. Veeam reads a Windows server's state over WMI. Next: Check WMI and DCOM on the server, and the account's rights. Source: Veeam KB1926.

Tools > Guided Diagnostics > Application-aware processing of SQL Server fails

Application-aware processing of SQL Server fails

A job's guest processing of SQL Server fails or truncates no logs.

Before You Begin

Run it on. On the SQL Server host whose guest processing fails. The service, VSS writer and event log steps read the machine SAT runs on, and the permission steps sign in to the instance named in the field. Run SAT as the account the job uses for guest processing, or type that account in Another account.

  • To run steps 3 and 4, have the instance name as clients connect to it first, such as SQLHOST01\INSTANCE, or the host name alone for the default instance, on the SQL Server host.
  • To check the rights of the account the job uses for guest processing, start SAT first as that account, on the SQL Server host. Steps 3 and 4 sign in to the instance with Windows authentication as the account running SAT.
  • Optional: to read another account's rights in step 3, start SAT first as an account that holds VIEW ANY DEFINITION or sysadmin on the instance, and type the account in Another account, on the SQL Server host. Without that right the other account's rows cannot be seen.
  • To read the SQL Server VSS writer in step 2, start SAT first as administrator, on the SQL Server host. Without it step 2 reads Could not check.
  • To sign in to the instance in steps 3 and 4 with a current driver, install Microsoft's ODBC Driver 18 or 17 for SQL Server first, on the SQL Server host. Without either, the older SQL Server driver included with Windows is used.
To run the scenario, do the following:
  1. In Customer / Lab, open Tools > Guided Diagnostics and choose Application-aware processing of SQL Server fails.
  2. Fill in the options. The table below describes each.
  3. Tick Keep going after a failure to run every step.
  4. Choose Run scenario.
  5. Copy the Result and Case note rows into the case note.
Expected result. Each step reads Pass, Attention, Fail, Not applicable, Could not check or Not run, with what it means and what to do next.

Options.

OptionWhat it does
SQL Server / instanceRequired. The instance whose guest processing fails, as clients connect to it, such as SQLHOST01\INSTANCE; the host name alone is the default instance. Steps 3 and 4 sign in to it, and step 1 reads its service when it is this machine. Left empty, steps 1, 3 and 4 read Could not check.
Another accountOptional. An account whose rights step 3 reads from the instance's catalog rows, such as the one the job uses for guest processing when SAT runs as someone else. The account running SAT needs VIEW ANY DEFINITION or sysadmin to see them, and rights an account gets through a Windows group are not counted. Left empty, the account running SAT is checked.
Keep going after a failureOptional. Ticked, every step runs and each failure is listed. Cleared, the run stops at the first failure of a step marked as stopping the run, and the steps after it read Not run.
StepWhat it checksWhat the result means
1. SQL Server serviceReads the Windows service of the instance on this machine from the Service Control Manager: MSSQLSERVER for the default instance, MSSQL$NAME for a named one. A running service passes; a service that is not installed, is disabled, or is not running although set to start automatically fails; a stopped service set to manual start is reported without a failure. When the field names another machine the step reads Not applicable. A failure here stops the run.Fail. Application-aware processing needs the SQL Server instance running. Next: Start the SQL Server service, and enable it first when it is disabled, then rerun the job. A service that is not installed means the instance name does not match an instance on this machine.
2. SQL Server VSS writerAsks the Volume Shadow Copy Service for the state of every VSS writer on this machine, without taking a snapshot, and looks at SqlServerWriter. It passes when the writer is Stable with no error code; a writer in any other state, with an error code, or missing from the list fails. Reading the writers needs SAT run as administrator, and the step reads Could not check when they cannot be read. A failure here stops the run.Fail. A failed SqlServerWriter stops the snapshot of the databases. Next: Restart the SQL Server VSS Writer service and read the Application log events it left.
3. Guest processing account rightsSigns in to the instance with Windows authentication as the account running SAT, or reads the catalog rows of the account in Another account, and compares its rights with the Veeam Permissions page: membership of sysadmin, or the minimal list. The minimal list is the server roles public and dbcreator; VIEW ANY DEFINITION, VIEW SERVER STATE and CONNECT SQL; and roles in model (db_backupoperator, db_denydatareader, public), master (db_backupoperator, db_datareader, public) and msdb (db_backupoperator, db_datareader, public, db_datawriter). Another account is read only when the signed-in account holds VIEW ANY DEFINITION or sysadmin, and rights it gets through a Windows group are not counted. A named account with no login on the instance fails when the signed-in account can see the logins. A failure here stops the run.Fail. The account used for application-aware processing needs sysadmin, or the minimal set the guide lists. Next: The database administrator grants the missing rights; rerun the job. Source: Permissions (Veeam Backup & Replication 13 User Guide), Veeam KB2689.
Attention. The account is not a member of sysadmin but holds the minimal list, which the Permissions page gives as the alternative. Source: Permissions (Veeam Backup & Replication 13 User Guide).
4. NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM fallbackRuns the same comparison for the account NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM from the instance's catalog rows. The signed-in account sees those rows only with VIEW ANY DEFINITION or sysadmin, and rights SYSTEM gets through a Windows group are not counted.Fail. When the account lacks rights, Veeam tries NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, which then needs them. Next: Grant the rights to the processing account, not to SYSTEM. Source: Veeam KB2027.
Attention. NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM is not a member of sysadmin but holds the minimal list.
5. SQL writer eventsReads the Application event log on this machine for the last 7 days and counts the events with id 24582 or 1 from the providers SQLWRITER and SQLVDI, of any severity. Any such event needs attention, and the row shows the newest.Attention. Events from SQLWRITER or SQLVDI with these ids usually come with a failed SQL snapshot. Next: Read the events' text for the database and the cause.

SQL transaction log backup fails or the chain is broken

Log backups fail, or a restore says the logs do not match a backup.

Before You Begin

Run it on. On the SQL Server host, or on any machine that reaches the instance over ODBC with an account that can sign in to it. Both steps connect to the instance named in the field, so the machine SAT runs on only has to reach it.

  • To run both steps, have the instance name as clients connect to it first, such as SQLHOST01\INSTANCE, on the machine running SAT.
  • To read the backup history in step 1, start SAT first as an account that can sign in to the instance and read msdb's backup history, on the SQL Server host or any machine that reaches the instance. Both steps sign in with Windows authentication as the account running SAT.
  • To sign in to the instance with a current driver, install Microsoft's ODBC Driver 18 or 17 for SQL Server first, on the machine running SAT. Without either, the older SQL Server driver included with Windows is used.
To run the scenario, do the following:
  1. In Customer / Lab, open Tools > Guided Diagnostics and choose SQL transaction log backup fails or the chain is broken.
  2. Fill in the options. The table below describes each.
  3. Tick Keep going after a failure to run every step.
  4. Choose Run scenario.
  5. Copy the Result and Case note rows into the case note.
Expected result. Each step reads Pass, Attention, Fail, Not applicable, Could not check or Not run, with what it means and what to do next.

Options.

OptionWhat it does
SQL Server / instanceRequired. The instance whose log backups fail, as clients connect to it, such as SQLHOST01\INSTANCE. Both steps sign in to it. Left empty, both steps read Could not check.
DatabaseOptional. The database whose backup history step 1 reads. Step 2 reads the whole instance. Left empty, step 1 reads every database except tempdb.
DaysOptional. How many days of msdb's backup history step 1 reads. A value below 1 or one that is not a number is read as 1, and a value above 3650 as 3650. Default 14.
Keep going after a failureOptional. Ticked, every step runs and each failure is listed. Cleared, the run stops at the first failure of a step marked as stopping the run, and the steps after it read Not run.
StepWhat it checksWhat the result means
1. Backups and the log chainSigns in to the instance's msdb database with Windows authentication as the account running SAT and reads each database's recovery model and msdb's backup history for the last Days days (14 by default), for the database named or every database except tempdb. For each database it counts full, copy-only full, differential and log backups and who took each: Veeam, recognised by a software or device name that names Veeam or by the vendor id seen with it; likely Veeam for a VSS snapshot full where Veeam is installed on the SQL host or the database has Veeam backups; SQL Server itself; or another product. It checks that each log backup starts where the one before it ended, and lists the log chain oldest first. The step fails on a log backup that is not copy-only and not Veeam's, for a database that also has Veeam backups in the days read; on a log backup to NUL; on a gap in the log chain that is not followed by a new chain; and on a database in the full or bulk-logged recovery model that cannot take a log backup until a full backup exists. A failure here stops the run.Fail. A log backup outside Veeam that is not copy-only, a log backup to NUL, a gap in the log chain, or a database with no full backup to log from breaks the chain Veeam's log backups depend on. Next: Make other backups copy-only, then run the Veeam job so it starts a new chain. For a database with no full backup, run a full backup first. Source: Veeam KB2117, Veeam KB2027.
Attention. The history shows a full backup outside Veeam that is not copy-only, a log chain broken and started again with a new full, a restarted log chain, a changed recovery model, a restore, or a log waiting for a log backup that was not taken. Each row names the database and, where the history gives one, the time. Next: Check that each of these was expected.
2. Availability groups and backup preferenceReads from the instance whether it is a failover cluster instance, with its nodes and shared disks, and whether Always On is enabled. For each availability group it reads the replicas with their roles, synchronization health and backup priority, the listener, the backup preference and the databases this node is the preferred backup replica for. A replica whose reported synchronization health is not HEALTHY needs attention.Attention. A replica of an availability group reports a synchronization health other than HEALTHY. Veeam processes a node only when its backup preference allows it, and takes the logs from one node per interval. Next: Check the replica's health and the group's backup preference against the job. Source: Always On Availability Groups support (Veeam Backup & Replication 13 User Guide).

OptionWhat it does

1. BottleneckCompares the busy percentages typed from the job's statistics for Source, Proxy, Network and Target and names the highest as the bottleneck; with equal figures the first of the four in that order is named. With at least one number it reads Attention, since it names the busiest component; with none typed it reads Could not check.Attention. Fast Clone cannot be confirmed on this volume: ReFS without block cloning, XFS without reflink or CRC, with a block size outside 1 KB to 4 KB or with settings that could not be read, or a network share whose Fast Clone depends on the server. Certificate or TLS error between Veeam components

A component reports a certificate, trust or TLS error when connecting.

Before You Begin

Run it on. On the machine that reports the error, the client side of the connection, with the server it connects to in the field. On a Windows backup server with no expected certificate typed, the certificate is compared with the one Veeam Backup & Replication is configured with. On any other machine, type the expected fingerprint to compare one.

  • To run steps 1 to 3, have the server's name or address, as the failing component uses it, and the port of the Veeam service that reports the error, such as 9401, first, on the machine that reports the error.
  • Optional: to compare the certificate with a known one in step 3, have its SHA-1 or SHA-256 fingerprint ready first, from the machine that holds the certificate. Without one, step 3 completes the handshake and reads the certificate.
  • To test another server's certificate from a Windows backup server, type that certificate's fingerprint first, on the backup server. An empty fingerprint there is compared with the certificate Veeam Backup & Replication is configured with, and step 3 fails when the two differ.
To run the scenario, do the following:
  1. In Customer / Lab, open Tools > Guided Diagnostics and choose Certificate or TLS error between Veeam components.
  2. Fill in the options. The table below describes each.
  3. Tick Keep going after a failure to run every step.
  4. Choose Run scenario.
  5. Copy the Result and Case note rows into the case note.
Expected result. Each step reads Pass, Attention, Fail, Not applicable, Could not check or Not run, with what it means and what to do next.

Options.

OptionWhat it does
Server name or addressRequired. The server the failing component connects to, by the name that component uses for it. Steps 1 to 3 all use it. Left empty, they read Could not check.
PortOptional. The TCP port of the Veeam service that reports the error. Step 3 runs the TLS handshake on it. Default 9401.
Expected certificate SHA-1/SHA-256 (optional)Optional. The SHA-1 or SHA-256 fingerprint of the certificate the server should present, with or without colons or spaces. Step 3 fails when the certificate differs. Left empty on a Windows backup server, step 3 expects the certificate Veeam Backup & Replication is configured with, which suits the backup server's own port and fails for another server's certificate; left empty elsewhere, it reads the certificate without a comparison.
Keep going after a failureOptional. Ticked, every step runs and each failure is listed. Cleared, the run stops at the first failure of a step marked as stopping the run, and the steps after it read Not run.
StepWhat it checksWhat the result means
1. Name resolutionLooks the name up the way this machine does: the hosts file first, then each DNS server this machine is configured with, asking each for the IPv4 and then the IPv6 addresses. The addresses in the row are the ones this machine's resolver returns, and the row says where the answer came from first. A typed IP address passes. The step fails when the resolver returns no address. A failure here stops the run.Fail. The certificate is checked against the name the component connects to. Next: Correct the DNS record or the hosts entry.
Attention. The hosts file has an entry for this name and a DNS server also answers for it, or the DNS servers answer with different addresses, so the name can lead to a machine other than the one intended. Next: Compare the addresses with the server's current address, then correct the hosts entry or the DNS record.

A difference over 1 minute needs attention and over 5 minutes fails. A server that does not answer SNTP reads Could not check.Fail. A certificate is valid only between its dates, on both machines' clocks. The clocks differ by more than 5 minutes. Next: Correct the time source of the machine that is off.
Attention. A certificate is valid only between its dates, on both machines' clocks. The clocks differ by more than a minute. Next: Correct the time source of the machine that is off.

TLS handshakeConnects to the server on the port given, waiting up to 10 seconds for the connection and again for the handshake, offers TLS 1.2 and 1.3, and reads the certificate the server presents: subject, issuer, expiry and SHA-256 fingerprint, with the TLS version and cipher agreed. The handshake completes whatever the certificate's trust, name or dates, so those are for the engineer to read in the row. With an expected fingerprint typed, the certificate has to match it. With none typed on a Windows backup server, the expected certificate is the one Veeam Backup & Replication is configured with, found in the LocalMachine Personal certificate store by the thumbprint Veeam Backup & Replication records (BackupServerCertificateThumbprint), or the store's Veeam Backup Server Certificate when none is recorded. A connection that cannot be made, or a handshake that does not complete, fails the step. A failure here stops the run.Fail. The connection, the handshake or the expected certificate failed. Veeam components connect with TLS and check the certificate the server presents. Next: If the row names a connection failure, check the port and the firewall first. Otherwise compare the certificate shown with the one the client expects; renew or replace it on the server. A Veeam task, service or console fails with The RPC server is unavailable, Only one usage of each socket address, or a connection that cannot be made, and a process cannot open another socket or port.

  • To read the Windows event logs and the process handle counts in full, start SAT first as administrator, on the machine that fails. Without it, a step that cannot read a log or a process reads Could not check, or counts only what it can see.
  • To see the ports in use at the time of the failure, run the scenario while the failure is happening, on the machine that fails. Steps 3 and 4 read the sockets of the moment they run.
  • Optional: to run step 10, note the name or address of the machine the failing RPC call goes to, from the job's error text, on the backup server. Without it step 10 reads Could not check and the other steps still run.
To run the scenario, do the following:
  1. In Customer / Lab, open Tools > Guided Diagnostics and choose RPC or port exhaustion.
  2. Fill in the options. The table below describes each.
  3. Tick Keep going after a failure to run every step.
  4. Choose Run scenario.

OptionWhat it does

1. Dynamic port range and TIME_WAIT delayReads the TCP and UDP dynamic port ranges from the network stack through WMI in the root\StandardCimv2 namespace (MSFT_NetTCPSetting for the Internet setting, and MSFT_NetUDPSetting), and the registry values MaxUserPort and TcpTimedWaitDelay under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters. A missing TcpTimedWaitDelay reads as the default of 240 seconds. The row gives each range with its first port, last port and size, and the number of new connections per second the TCP range allows, which is its size divided by the TIME_WAIT delay. Ranges of 16,384 ports or more that are the same for TCP and UDP and start at 49152 or higher, with a delay of 30 to 240 seconds, pass. A smaller range, a start below 49152, ranges that differ, a delay outside 30 to 240 seconds, or a MaxUserPort that is not the last port of the TCP range needs attention. A range under 5,000 ports fails. A Windows version without the root\StandardCimv2 namespace reads Could not check.Fail. Only a few ports are available for outgoing connections. Each new connection needs one until it is released, and the Windows default is 16,384. Next: Restore the default range, then run the scenario again. A wider range gives time and does not remove the cause. Source: Default dynamic port range for TCP/IP (Microsoft), TCP/IP port exhaustion troubleshooting (Microsoft), MSFT_NetTCPSetting class (Microsoft).
Attention. The range is smaller than the default, starts below 49152, differs between TCP and UDP, or the delay is not the default. A range that starts below 49152 moves the ports RPC uses outside the range Veeam asks firewalls to open, and a smaller range or a longer delay lowers how fast the machine can reuse ports. Next: Check the firewall rules and the RPC settings against a changed range first. Source: Default dynamic port range for TCP/IP (Microsoft), Veeam KB4760, Veeam KB4217.
2. Port exhaustion eventsReads the System event log on this machine for the last 7 days and counts the events with id 4231, 4227 or 4266 from the provider Tcpip. 4231 is a failed request for a TCP port because all were in use, 4227 is a connection that reused a local port too soon for the same remote endpoint, and 4266 is a failed request for a UDP port. Any such event in the last 7 days needs attention, and a 4231 within the last 24 hours fails the step. The row gives the count of each and the time of the newest.Fail. A request for a TCP port failed within the last 24 hours because all ports were in use. Next: Read steps 3 and 4 to see which process holds the ports, and run the scenario again while the failure is happening. Source: TCP/IP port exhaustion troubleshooting (Microsoft).
Attention. A port exhaustion event was logged. 4231 means a request for a TCP port failed because all were in use. 4227 means a connection reused a local port too soon for the same remote endpoint, which happens when connections open and close at a high rate. 4266 is the same failure for UDP and also appears on machines that work normally, so read it with steps 3 and 4. Next: Compare the time of the newest event with the time of the failure, then read steps 3 and 4. Source: TCP/IP port exhaustion troubleshooting (Microsoft), Event ID 4227, Tcpip (Microsoft).
3. Ports in use against the rangeReads this machine's TCP and UDP socket tables, the ones the Local Port Checker reads, and counts the distinct local ports inside each dynamic range on the local address that holds the most. A socket bound to every address holds its port on each address. The row gives the count, its share of the range and the sockets by state for TCP, the same for UDP, and the same for TCP ports 2500 to 3300, the range the Veeam ports page lists for data movers. Under 50 percent of every range passes, 50 to 89 percent of one needs attention and 90 percent or more of one fails. Ports in the BOUND state are not in the socket tables, so the counts are a lower bound, and the tables are a snapshot of the moment the step runs.Fail. A range is nearly full. At exhaustion one or two processes usually hold 90 to 95 percent of it, and a new outgoing connection fails when no port is free. Next: Read step 4 for the process that holds the ports. A wider range gives time and does not remove the cause. Source: Port Exhaustion and You (Microsoft Directory Services team), TCP/IP port exhaustion troubleshooting (Microsoft).
Attention. A range is half used or more. A process that keeps opening connections uses a range up, and new outgoing connections fail when it is full. Next: Read step 4 for the process that holds the ports, and run the scenario again while the failure is happening. Source: Port Exhaustion and You (Microsoft Directory Services team), TCP/IP port exhaustion troubleshooting (Microsoft), Ports (Veeam Backup & Replication 13 User Guide).
4. Which process holds the portsGroups the TCP sockets inside the dynamic range by the process that owns them and lists the five that hold the most, with the process name, its PID, the Windows services it hosts, its ports and its share of the sockets in the range, and the processes with sockets in CLOSE_WAIT. Sockets in TIME_WAIT have no owner, so the row lists the three remote endpoints with the most of them, and the process with the most live connections to the same endpoint as the likely one. A process named in Process name or PID is reported beside them, all instances of a name together. With the ports in use at 50 percent of the range or more and one process holding half of the sockets in it, the step needs attention, and at 90 percent or more it fails. A process with 500 or more sockets in CLOSE_WAIT, or one remote endpoint with half of 1,000 or more TIME_WAIT sockets, needs attention.Fail. One process holds half of the sockets of a range that is almost full. Next: Contact the vendor of the process. For a Veeam program, collect its logs for the time of the failure and open a case. Source: Port Exhaustion and You (Microsoft Directory Services team), TCP/IP port exhaustion troubleshooting (Microsoft).
Attention. One process holds half of the sockets in the range, keeps many sockets in CLOSE_WAIT, or many short connections go to one remote endpoint. A process that keeps this many ports open is busy or does not close its sockets. Many short connections to one endpoint use the range faster than TIME_WAIT frees it. Next: Compare the process's handle count in step 5. For a Veeam program, collect its logs for the time of the failure and open a case. For connections to one endpoint, compare the rate with step 1. Source: Port Exhaustion and You (Microsoft Directory Services team), TCP/IP port exhaustion troubleshooting (Microsoft), Veeam KB4760.
5. Handles and kernel poolReads the open handle count of each process, and the kernel pool sizes from the system's performance information: nonpaged pool, paged pool, physical memory and the total handles of the system. The row lists the five processes with the most handles, leaving out System, lsass.exe, store.exe, sqlservr.exe and sqlsvr.exe, whose counts are normally high. A process at 3,000 handles or more, or nonpaged pool at 10 percent or more of physical memory, needs attention. A process at 10,000 handles or more that is also the process holding the most ports in step 4, or holds 20 percent or more of the sockets in the range, fails.Fail. A process with more than 10,000 handles also holds the most ports, or a fifth of them. That is the pattern of a process that opens sockets and does not close them. Next: Contact the vendor of the process. For a Veeam program, collect its logs for the time of the failure and open a case. Source: TCP/IP port exhaustion troubleshooting (Microsoft), Port Exhaustion and You (Microsoft Directory Services team).
Attention. A process holds many handles, or the nonpaged pool is large. On a machine that cannot make outgoing connections the process at fault often has more than 10,000 handles, and most of them are sockets. Handle counts include files and other objects, so read this with step 4. A port needs a handle from nonpaged pool, so an exhausted pool gives the same symptom as exhausted ports. Next: Read step 4 for the process, and step 6 for pool events. For a large nonpaged pool, look for the driver or program that leaks pool memory. Source: TCP/IP port exhaustion troubleshooting (Microsoft), Port Exhaustion and You (Microsoft Directory Services team).
6. Pool exhaustion eventsReads the System event log on this machine for the last 7 days and counts the events with id 2019 or 2020 from the provider Srv: the Server service could not allocate from the nonpaged pool (2019) or the paged pool (2020) because the pool was empty. Any such event needs attention, and one within the last 24 hours fails the step.Fail. The Server service could not get memory from a system pool within the last 24 hours because the pool was empty. An empty pool also stops new sockets, so it looks like port exhaustion. Next: Look for the driver or program that leaks pool memory, and read step 5. Source: Unable to allocate memory from the system paged pool (Microsoft), Port Exhaustion and You (Microsoft Directory Services team).
Attention. The Server service could not get memory from a system pool because the pool was empty. An empty pool also stops new sockets, so it looks like port exhaustion. Next: Look for the driver or program that leaks pool memory, and read step 5. Source: Unable to allocate memory from the system paged pool (Microsoft), Port Exhaustion and You (Microsoft Directory Services team).
7. RPC servicesReads the Service Control Manager state of RpcSs (Remote Procedure Call), RpcEptMapper (RPC Endpoint Mapper) and DcomLaunch. All three running passes. A service that is not installed, is disabled, or is not running although it starts automatically fails the step, and one that is stopped with manual start needs attention. A failure here stops the run.Fail. An RPC service is missing, disabled or stopped. RPC cannot register or find endpoints without these services, so the steps after this one are not meaningful. Next: Read the System event log for the reason the service stopped, and correct it with the machine's administrator. Source: Service overview and network port requirements for Windows (Microsoft).
Attention. An RPC service is stopped and set to start manually. RPC cannot register or find endpoints while a service it needs is stopped. Next: Read the System event log for the reason the service is stopped. Source: Service overview and network port requirements for Windows (Microsoft).
8. RPC dynamic port restrictionReads the registry key HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Rpc\Internet in the 64-bit view: the values Ports (a list of ports and ranges such as 5000-5100), PortsInternetAvailable and UseInternetPorts. Without the key RPC is not restricted and takes its ports from the dynamic range in step 1, which passes. With a Ports list the row counts the ports and how many of them a TCP socket holds. A list with fewer than 100 ports, or an entry that is not a port or a range of 0 to 65535, fails. A list of 100 ports or more with 80 percent or more of them in use, or PortsInternetAvailable and UseInternetPorts that disagree, needs attention. A Netlogon event 5820 in the last 7 days is added to the row.Fail. RPC is limited to too few ports, or the list cannot be read. Microsoft's guidance is at least 100 ports, because several system services use them. With too few ports, or an entry RPC cannot read, the endpoint mapper cannot register servers. Next: Correct the Ports value as the Microsoft page describes. Source: Configure RPC dynamic port allocation to work with firewalls (Microsoft), Veeam KB1174.
Attention. Most of the ports RPC may use are in use, or the default policy points at ports outside the list. Computers with high traffic can run out of RPC ports when the list is short. Next: Widen the list or remove the restriction as the Microsoft page describes, and keep the firewall rules in step with it. Source: Configure RPC dynamic port allocation to work with firewalls (Microsoft), Veeam KB1174.
9. Windows Firewall for RPCReads the Windows Defender Firewall service (mpssvc), the profiles in force with their inbound defaults, and the inbound rules. For each active profile it tests inbound TCP 135 for the RPC endpoint mapper, with the program and service that listen on it, and inbound TCP to the dynamic range from step 1 against the rules that name RPC Dynamic Ports, a range that holds the dynamic range, or any port. A profile with the firewall off passes. A profile that blocks inbound by default with no allow rule for 135 or for the dynamic range, or a block rule that covers either, fails. An active Public profile, group policy that manages the rules, or a third-party firewall that Windows reports needs attention, and a third-party firewall is named and not read. The rules read are those of this machine, so a firewall between two machines is not visible here.Fail. The firewall blocks inbound RPC on an active profile, so a remote RPC call to this machine cannot complete. Veeam components such as the guest interaction proxy reach a Windows guest on TCP 135 and, for Hyper-V and application-aware processing, on the dynamic RPC range. Next: Allow the RPC Endpoint Mapper and RPC Dynamic Ports inbound rules for the profile, or restore the default firewall settings. Source: Create inbound rules to support RPC (Microsoft), Veeam KB1174, Ports (Veeam Backup & Replication 13 User Guide).
Attention. Veeam lists a network on the Public location as a cause of error 1722. Group policy can change the rules read here, and another firewall in use is not read. Next: Set the network location that fits the network, and compare group policy and any other firewall with the rules shown. Source: Veeam KB1174, Create inbound rules to support RPC (Microsoft).
10. RPC endpoint mapper on the other machineConnects from this machine to TCP port 135 on the server in Remote server for the RPC test and sends a DCE/RPC bind request to the RPC endpoint mapper, which a working RPC service answers with a bind acknowledgement. Each stage waits up to 5 seconds, and the row names the stage that failed, the connection or the bind. Only port 135 is tested. The dynamic port a call is sent to afterwards is outside this step. Left empty, the step reads Could not check.Fail. The server did not accept a bind on port 135. Error 1722, The RPC server is unavailable, is logged when a lower layer cannot connect: name resolution, a blocked port 135, or a service that is not running on the server. Next: Run this scenario on the server to read its own ports, and check the firewalls on the path. Source: RPC error 1722, the RPC server is unavailable (Microsoft), Veeam KB1174, Veeam KB1926.
Every step reads only. No step repairs WMI, restarts a service, changes a firewall, grants a right or changes the configuration database; the result names the guide section, and the customer's administrator acts.

Related topics

Guided Diagnostics Overview
Tools > Network Tools

Network Tools

Network Tools tests the paths between Veeam components: ports, names, TLS, RPC, gRPC, SMB, listeners for another machine to test against, packet capture and throughput. The page groups its tools in three sections.

Connectivity and protocols

  • Remote Port Checker: Ports on another host: TCP or UDP over IPv4 and IPv6, where the name resolved from, the route from each local interface, and SAT-to-SAT verification.
  • Local Port Checker (F6): Ports on this machine: the process on each, and the firewall's verdict.
  • Name Check (F2): What a name resolves to here, and where the answer came from.
  • File Transfer Calculator (F10): How long a transfer takes over a link, worked out step by step, with text for an email.
  • TLS Handshake: The TLS negotiation, the certificate the server presents and the protocol details, apart from any application.
  • Windows RPC Connectivity: TCP reachability and a DCE/RPC Endpoint Mapper exchange. An open TCP/135 alone is not RPC success.
  • gRPC Connectivity: TCP, optional TLS and ALPN, HTTP/2 and the gRPC transport, with no service definition needed.
  • Veeam Service Channel: The channel Veeam's own processes use to reach their service: the service, its pipe, an HTTP/2 handshake and the gRPC lines the product logged.
  • SMB Connectivity: TCP/445, SMB negotiation, access to a path and a bounded write, read and delete, outside Veeam.

Listeners and peer tests

  • TCP / UDP Listener: Listens for test probes from another machine and records each one.
  • Local Loopback Self-Test: This machine's TCP loopback, through a temporary SAT listener on a free port.
  • gRPC Listener: A SAT HTTP/2 and gRPC listener for a gRPC Connectivity test from another machine.

Capture and performance

  • Packet Capture: Network traffic captured into the case's Log-Collections folder with pktmon, or netsh on Windows Server 2016.
  • Network Throughput: TCP throughput between two SAT machines, with SAT's own client and server or iPerf3.

Local Port Checker, Name Check and the File Transfer Calculator open in their own windows, from this page or by their keys anywhere in SAT. The other tools open a form in a tab on the page.

To run a network tool, do the following:
  1. Open Tools > Network Tools.
  2. Choose the tool's card.
  3. Fill the form and choose its action. The table lists each check with its status; select a row to read it in full.
