Tools > Network Tools > Remote Port Checker

Remote Port Checker

Use the Remote Port Checker to test whether this machine can reach a port on another machine. It is two operations on Network Tools, TCP connectivity test and UDP connectivity test, each with its own fields and its own results. The Local Port Checker (F6) reads the ports on this machine instead. TCP and UDP report differently; see Understanding UDP results.

Before you start

  • To run a TCP test, make sure the port accepts connections from this machine through every firewall between the two machines. Nothing has to be started on the other machine.
  • To send the payload to a SAT listener (Validate an in-memory payload when peer is a SAT listener), start a TCP listener first, on the other machine: in SAT open Tools > Network Tools, choose TCP listener, set Listen port to the port tested and Duration seconds to cover the test, and choose Listen. Run the test from this machine afterwards.
  • To let the test connect more than once, tick Accept multiple connections until timeout on that listener first, on the other machine. The test connects once for each address family of the name and once for each adapter chosen, and a listener that stops after its first connection is closed to the others.
  • To get a VERIFIED UDP result, start a UDP listener first, on the other machine: choose UDP listener, set Listen port to the port tested and Duration seconds to cover the test, and choose Listen UDP. Then tick Verify a cooperating SAT UDP listener on this machine and run the test. A UDP test with no answer reads INDETERMINATE, as UDP has no handshake.
  • To let a listener accept the test, allow SAT when Windows asks whether it may listen on the network, first, on the machine with the listener. Allow it for the network this machine connects over. The answer stays as a firewall rule.

The form

Both operations ask for a host, a port and a timeout, and send from the adapters ticked under those fields. The TCP connectivity test adds a payload size and a tick box to send it. The UDP connectivity test adds a tick box to verify a SAT UDP listener.

ControlUsed inWhat it does
HostTCP and UDPThe name or IP address of the machine to test. Starts as localhost. Choose... lists the machines of the active case and the addresses saved in Settings.
PortTCP and UDPThe port to connect to or send to, from 1 to 65535. Starts as 2500. Choose... lists Veeam's ports by number with the role that uses each.
Timeout msTCP and UDPIn the TCP connectivity test, how long to wait for each connection attempt, in milliseconds. Starts as 5000. In the UDP connectivity test, how long to wait for an answer. Starts as 2000.
Payload MiBTCPHow much data to send when the payload tick box is ticked, as a whole number from 1 to 8192 (1024 is a gigabyte). Starts as 50 and is not read while that box is clear.
Validate an in-memory payload when peer is a SAT listenerTCPTicked, a test against a SAT listener also sends Payload MiB of data from memory and compares the byte count and SHA-256 at both ends, which gives a rough bandwidth reading. Clear to begin with, so a plain port test sends no payload. See In-Memory Payload Validation.
Verify a cooperating SAT UDP listener (required for PASS)UDPTicked, the probe expects an acknowledgement from a SAT UDP listener on the other machine, which is the only way the result reads VERIFIED. Clear, a probe with no answer reads INDETERMINATE. Clear to begin with.
Send from these adaptersTCP and UDPOne tick box for each adapter that is up and has an address, followed by its IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and marked [VLAN], [TEAM/BOND] or [VIRTUAL] where that applies. The test runs from each ticked adapter, once for each of its addresses in the ticked families, so the rows show which adapter reached the target and which did not. Adapters start ticked, except virtual adapters and adapters with only a link-local address, which start clear; when no adapter qualifies, all start ticked. The list shows the first 12 adapters. With none ticked, Windows chooses the route.
IPv4 and IPv6TCP and UDPTwo tick boxes under the adapter list, both ticked to begin with. They choose which address families a ticked adapter sends from, and are not repeated for each adapter.

A target of localhost or another loopback address (127.0.0.1 or ::1) in the TCP connectivity test uses the Windows loopback path. Loopback traffic does not leave through an adapter, so the ticked adapters are not used. The IPv4 and IPv6 boxes then choose which loopback addresses are tested, and localhost tests both. To test a particular adapter, enter that adapter's own IP address as the host.

To run a TCP connectivity test, do the following:
  1. Open Tools > Network Tools and choose TCP connectivity test.
  2. Enter Host and Port. Change Timeout ms for a slow link.
  3. Under Send from these adapters, leave the adapters ticked to test from each, tick only the adapters to compare, or clear them all to let Windows choose the route.
  4. Tick Validate an in-memory payload when peer is a SAT listener and set Payload MiB only when a SAT TCP listener is running on the target.
  5. Choose Test TCP.
  6. Read the rows under Reading the result rows.
Result. Each address tried reads CONNECTED, or FAILED with the reason the socket reported, such as refused, timed out or unreachable. A successful TCP connect confirms the socket path only; use payload validation or TLS Handshake when the application layer also needs testing.
To run a UDP connectivity test, do the following:
  1. Open Tools > Network Tools and choose UDP connectivity test.
  2. Enter Host and Port. Change Timeout ms to wait longer for an answer.
  3. Choose the adapters under Send from these adapters as for the TCP connectivity test.
  4. Tick Verify a cooperating SAT UDP listener (required for PASS) only when a SAT UDP listener is running on the target.
  5. Choose Test UDP.
Result. An acknowledgement from a SAT UDP listener reads VERIFIED. A probe with no answer reads INDETERMINATE: UDP gives no sign that a datagram arrived.

Reading the result rows

The results list has four columns: Protocol, IP Address, Details and Result. The rows come in this order.

ProtocolResultWhat the row says
ROUTING, TARGET, NEXTLOOPBACK, NORMALIZED, GUIDANCEFirst, for a loopback target in the TCP connectivity test: that the Windows loopback path was used, that localhost was tested as its loopback addresses, and, when adapters were ticked, that they were not used and what to enter to test one.
DNSSOURCEWhere the name resolved from: the hosts file and the line of the entry, a DNS server and the adapter it belongs to, this machine for localhost, or the DNS cache, LLMNR, mDNS or NetBIOS when neither the hosts file nor a configured DNS server gave the answer.
DNSRESOLVEDOne row for each address the name resolved to, named IPv4 or IPv6, with the canonical name when there is one. A host entered as an IP address has one row reading NOT REQUIRED, as no lookup is made.
IPv4, IPv6CONNECTED, FAILED, NOT TESTED, NO ADDRESSOne row for each address family, saying whether that family worked. CONNECTED gives the first address that connected, the time and the adapter, and adds SAT listener verified or SAT listener and payload verified when the target is a SAT listener. FAILED gives how many addresses were tried. NOT TESTED means the name has an address of that family and no test used it. NO ADDRESS means the name has no address of that family. In the UDP connectivity test these rows read VERIFIED, RESPONSE RECEIVED, INDETERMINATE or FAILED.
TCP or UDPCONNECTED, FAILED; VERIFIED, RESPONSE RECEIVED, INDETERMINATE, FAILEDOne row for each address tried: the port, the time in milliseconds and the source adapter with its address. A failed TCP attempt adds the error number and the reason the socket gave, such as refused or timed out.
TCP or UDPNOT TESTEDAn adapter whose addresses are of one family while the target has none of that family, for example an IPv6 adapter against a name that has only an IPv4 address. The row names the adapter and says what the target lacks.
SATVERIFIED, DETECTED, NO ACKAgainst a SAT listener: its Test ID. TCP reads VERIFIED when the SAT handshake completed and DETECTED when a SAT listener was recognised without completing it. UDP reads VERIFIED when the listener acknowledged the Test ID and NO ACK when it did not.
BANNERRECEIVEDThe text the TCP listener sent when the connection was accepted.
PAYLOADVERIFIEDThe size of the payload that was sent from memory and verified, with the transfer rate it reached.

A name is tested over both address families, so an IPv6 path that fails beside a working IPv4 one shows on its own row. A source adapter whose test could not run gets a FAILED row that names the adapter and the reason. The summary of the run says whether any tested path connected and, for a TCP test against a SAT listener, whether the payload was verified.

Understanding UDP results

UDP has no connection handshake, so a datagram that was sent and not answered shows nothing either way. The result is one of four.

  • VERIFIED. A SAT UDP listener on the other machine acknowledged the probe's Test ID. It needs the listener running there and Verify a cooperating SAT UDP listener ticked here.
  • RESPONSE RECEIVED. A reply came back that was not a SAT acknowledgement.
  • INDETERMINATE. The datagram was sent and nothing answered within Timeout ms. The port may be open, closed or filtered.
  • FAILED. The datagram could not be sent.

Use a cooperating SAT UDP Listener when you need a verified probe and acknowledgement.

Firewall rows on the listeners

The TCP listener and the UDP listener start with a FIREWALL row, NOTE, saying that Windows can ask whether to allow SupportAssistTool.exe the first time it listens on a network. When a listener stops, it lists one FIREWALL row for each firewall rule that names SAT, reading ALLOW or BLOCK, with rule disabled where that applies. Each of those rules stays until it is removed from Windows Defender Firewall. See TCP / UDP Listener.

Command line: network test --host HOST --port PORT and network udp test --host HOST --port PORT.

Results and history. Tools and Guided Diagnostics use a readable result-card history as the primary view. Protocol/tool identity, IP/item, details, and the textual outcome are separated and outcome text is color-coded. Re-running a tool appends a new run; use Reset Output only when you intentionally want to clear the visible history. Saved diagnostic tool outputs are not deleted by Reset Output.
Operation-specific history. In a tool that offers several operations, changing the operation does not reuse the previous operation's result rows. SAT retains each operation independently so returning to an earlier operation restores its previous output until you reset it.

In-Memory Payload Validation

A TCP port can accept a connection even when larger application payloads later fail. The optional payload validation tests that condition between two SAT hosts without creating a customer-data file. Its check box is clear until ticked, so a plain port test sends no payload.

Volatile test data. SAT generates the payload in bounded memory chunks, streams it to the cooperating SAT listener, hashes/counts it on both ends, and discards each chunk. No test file or persistent SAT certificate is created.
To validate the data path, do the following:
  1. Start a TCP SAT Listener on the destination host.
  2. On the source host, open Remote Port Checker.
  3. Select TCP, target the listener, and enable SAT-to-SAT verification.
  4. Enable in-memory payload validation.
  5. Run the test.
  6. Review bytes sent/received, SHA-256 verification, timing, and any reset/timeout failure point.
Result. PASS requires the SAT listener handshake, expected byte count, and matching payload hash. A simple TCP connect is not treated as an equivalent payload test.

Testing Across Local Interfaces

Use Test Across Local Interfaces when a host has several usable IP-bearing interfaces and you want to compare observed connectivity from each source address. This can help narrow routing, firewall, source-subnet, VLAN, or interface-selection symptoms.

SAT enumerates usable local interfaces and binds each test to that interface's source address. Where the operating system exposes it, the result also records the interface type, route/next hop, link state, and team/bond membership.

Do not interpret the matrix as switch configuration discovery. SAT can test OS-visible VLAN interfaces/subinterfaces, but it does not know an external switchport's VLAN/trunk configuration unless the host OS/driver exposes that information. For NIC teams/bonds, SAT tests the logical routable interface and can show member state; it does not disable team members or claim per-member path validation unless the OS genuinely permits that routing choice.
To compare a target across local interfaces, do the following:
  1. Enter the target and port in Remote Port Checker or TLS Handshake.
  2. Review the discovered interface/address checklist and tick each interface you want SAT to originate from.
  3. Include virtual/special interfaces only when they are relevant to the investigation. Leave all interfaces unchecked when you intentionally want Windows automatic routing.
  4. Run the test.
  5. Compare the result cards for source interface/address, destination IP, protocol result, timing, SAT acknowledgement/payload result, or TLS result.
Localhost and NIC selection. When the target is localhost, an IPv4 loopback address, or ::1, SAT uses the operating-system loopback route and ignores physical/virtual source-NIC selections. To validate a specific local NIC from the same machine, target that NIC's own IP address instead.

TCP connectivity test.

FieldWhat it does
HostRequired. The name or IP address of the machine to test. Starts as localhost.
PortRequired. The TCP port to connect to, from 1 to 65535. Starts as 2500.
Timeout msRequired. How long to wait for each connection attempt, in milliseconds. Starts as 5000.
Payload MiBOptional. How much data to send, in MiB, when the payload tick box is ticked: a whole number from 1 to 8192. Starts as 50 and is not read while that box is clear.
Validate an in-memory payload when peer is a SAT listenerOptional. Ticked, a test against a SAT listener also sends Payload MiB of data from memory and compares the byte count and SHA-256 at both ends, which gives a rough bandwidth reading. Clear to begin with.

UDP connectivity test.

FieldWhat it does
HostRequired. The name or IP address of the machine to test. Starts as localhost.
PortRequired. The UDP port to send to, from 1 to 65535. Starts as 2500.
Timeout msRequired. How long to wait for an answer, in milliseconds. Starts as 2000.
Verify a cooperating SAT UDP listener (required for PASS)Optional. Ticked, the probe expects an acknowledgement from a SAT UDP listener on the other machine, which is the only way the result reads VERIFIED. Cleared, a probe with no answer reads INDETERMINATE. Clear to begin with.

Tools > Network Tools > Local Port Checker (F6)

Local Port Checker (F6)

The Local Port Checker shows what listens on this machine's ports, which program owns each, and whether this machine's firewall lets connections in. It reads this machine's socket tables and firewall rules. Use it before a test from another machine, to see whether a Veeam port is open, held by another program or blocked. Open it with F6.

Before You Begin

  • The window opens in both roles.
  • Quick scan needs SAT running as administrator.
To check ports, do the following:
  1. Press F6, or choose Tools > Local Port Checker.
  2. Type the ports as a list or ranges, for example 6162, 2500-2510. Choose TCP, UDP or both. Or pick a Veeam role from the list: its ports are filled in and each port that only one version of Veeam Backup & Replication lists is marked VBR 12 only or VBR 13 only.
  3. Choose Check. To check the ports of a program, type a process name or PID and choose Its ports.
  4. Choose a row to see the program that owns the port and the firewall's verdict for each network profile.
  5. Choose Export... to save the ports as CSV or JSON.

Each port gets a verdict: Open, Open on some profiles, Blocked here, Local only, Closed, or Closed and blocked. A role's range, such as 2500 to 3300, shows as one row: the ports of it that are held and the program holding each, or None of the range is held. While a result is shown, the sockets and the firewall are read again every 5 seconds, so the listening state, the program and the verdict follow the machine. On a Windows backup server the role also lists the ports its Veeam services hold on the loopback address only, such as 9392 for the Veeam Backup Service; each reads Local only while its service runs.

To test a port from another machine, do the following:
  1. Select a port nothing listens on and choose Start listener in the panel on the right. SAT listens on it for 5 minutes and greets each connection with a line that names SAT and the port.
  2. Tick Quick scan before starting the listener to count the attempts that arrive at the port and those that never reach the listener.
  3. On the other machine, test the port with the Remote Port Checker. See Remote Port Checker.
  4. Choose Stop to end the listener sooner.
A test from this machine to itself goes around its own firewall. Only a test from the other machine proves the path between them.

Command line: network local-ports PORTS; network presets lists the role presets and marks the ports only VBR 12 or only VBR 13 lists.

Name Check (F2)

What a name resolves to on this machine and where the answer came from first: the hosts file or which DNS server. Each DNS server this machine uses is asked on its own, so servers that disagree show, and each address is looked up in reverse.

  • Check. Type a short name, a full name or an address, such as vbr01 or vbr01.corp.local, and press Check or Enter. The result shows the answer from the hosts file, from each DNS server this machine uses, and the reverse lookup of each address.
  • A port. Remote Port Checker opens the Remote Port Checker with the address found filled in, to test a port on it.
Each question is one small packet to a DNS server this machine uses.

Command line: network name NAME.

To check what a name resolves to, do the following:
  1. Press F2.
  2. Type a short name, a full name or an address, such as vbr01 or vbr01.corp.local.
  3. Press Check or Enter. The result shows the answer from the hosts file, from each DNS server this machine uses, and the reverse lookup of each address.
  4. To test a port on the address found, choose Remote Port Checker. It opens with the address filled in.

Tools > Network Tools > File Transfer Calculator (F10)

File Transfer Calculator (F10)

How long a transfer takes over a network link, worked out one step at a time: the link speed in bytes, less the Ethernet and TCP/IP overhead, per hour, then the size. Sizes are as Windows counts them (1 TB = 1,024 GB). Manual works from the figures typed; Live test measures them from this machine.

  • Manual. Type the data to move with its unit (MB to PB), the link speed with its unit and the packet size, then press Calculate. Link throttle, Compression, Network speed and Storage speed can stay as they are.
  • Link throttle. How much of the link the Veeam job gets, in percent: 100 when nothing throttles or shares it. A traffic rule of 500 Mb/s on a 1 Gb/s link is 50; two jobs under that rule at once get 25 each.
  • Compression. How much of the data is left to send after Veeam compresses it, in percent. In the Veeam console open a run of the job (Statistics) and divide Transferred by Read: Read 800 GB and Transferred 400 GB is 50.
  • Live test. Choose the adapter the transfer leaves by: its link speed and packet size fill in. Start SAT's listener on the other machine (F6), type that machine and press Measure, or choose iPerf3 under Using for a machine running an iPerf3 server.
  • Result. The side panel shows each speed as a bar, the email text and the terms. Copy for email gives the estimate and how it is worked out as text. Every estimate shown is recorded in Recent Activity once.

The three speeds

Link speed is the speed the link is sold or negotiated at, such as 10 Gb/s, and the calculator works from it on paper: the link in bytes, less the Ethernet and TCP/IP overhead for the packet size. Link throttle is the share of that link the Veeam job gets when a Veeam network traffic rule throttles it, or other traffic shares it. Network speed is what a test between the two machines measured, such as an iPerf3 run, which takes in everything between them. The time uses the lowest of the link (after overhead and the share), the network speed and the storage speed.

None of the three has a direction: the path between the two machines is the same both ways. The storage speed is the one with a direction. For a backup, the repository writes, so use a Disk Speed Test's Writes on the repository. For a restore, the repository reads and the production storage writes, so use the lower of the two. A result.json opened with Open a result... gives Writes for a repository and Reads for a source.

Command line: network transfer-time and network adapters.

To work out how long a transfer takes, do the following:
  1. Press F10 and choose Manual.
  2. Type the data to move with its unit, the link speed with its unit and the packet size.
  3. Leave Link throttle, Compression, Network speed and Storage speed as they are, or set them.
  4. Press Calculate. The estimate is worked out one step at a time, with the speeds beside it and the text for an email.
  5. Choose Live test to measure the figures from this machine.

TLS Handshake

Use the TLS test when a TCP port is reachable but you need to determine whether the secure channel can negotiate and which public certificate the endpoint presents.

Result areaExamples

ServerHelloNegotiated TLS version, selected cipher, selected group/handshake metadata.
CertificateSubject, SAN, issuer, validity, SHA-1/SHA-256 fingerprint, chain/system trust, hostname comparison where available.
Failure stageTCP, ClientHello/ServerHello negotiation, certificate validation, client-certificate request, or another observed handshake stage.
To inspect a TLS endpoint, do the following:
  1. Enter the target hostname and TLS port.
  2. Provide an expected public certificate fingerprint only when you have one to compare.
  3. Optionally enable Compare TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. A version that is intentionally disabled is reported as an observed availability/negotiation result, not automatically as a product fault.
  4. Optionally enable Test Across Local Interfaces.
  5. Run the test and review the handshake/certificate result.
Ciphers. The result shows what the client offered and what the server chose. Which protocols and ciphers Veeam supports is in Veeam's communication encryption reference, listed in Related Documentation.

HostRequired. The name or IP address of the server to run the handshake against.

Tools > Network Tools > Windows RPC Connectivity

Windows RPC Connectivity

Use this diagnostic when logs report RPC availability or endpoint errors and you need an independent Windows/network result outside Veeam. SAT checks the RPC Endpoint Mapper on TCP/135 and performs a bounded DCE/RPC bind exchange. An open TCP socket without a bind reads as TCP reachability only.

Before you start

  • To use Windows RPC Connectivity, choose a Windows computer as the target. Nothing has to be started on it: the test connects to its RPC Endpoint Mapper on TCP 135 and asks for a bind.
  • To get a bind, open TCP 135 from this machine to the target through every firewall between them, first. Services reached through RPC then use dynamic ports, which a firewall can still block after 135 passes.

The result separates DNS, TCP/135, Endpoint Mapper protocol response, native socket/RPC error information, what was proven, and suggested next checks. Dynamic service-specific RPC ports remain a separate layer and can still be blocked after TCP/135 succeeds.

To test Windows RPC connectivity, do the following:
  1. Open Tools > Network Tools in the Customer / Lab role and choose Windows RPC Connectivity.
  2. Type the Windows computer's name or address in Target host.
  3. Leave RPC Endpoint Mapper port at 135 and Timeout ms at 5000, or change them.
  4. Choose Test RPC. The result lists DNS, TCP 135, the Endpoint Mapper response, what was proven and the suggested next checks.
FieldWhat it does
Target hostRequired. The Windows computer to test: its name or IP address.
RPC Endpoint Mapper portRequired. The Endpoint Mapper port on the target. Starts as 135, the port Windows RPC uses.
Timeout msRequired. How long to wait for the bind exchange, in milliseconds. Starts as 5000.

Tools > Network Tools > gRPC Connectivity

gRPC Connectivity and gRPC Listener

Use the gRPC connectivity test to validate the transport layers required by gRPC without requiring an application-specific .proto, method, authentication flow, or Veeam service payload. SAT reports DNS/TCP, optional TLS and ALPN h2, HTTP/2 framing, and the first failed layer.

Before you start

  • To test a gRPC transport, have a gRPC or HTTP/2 service on the port tested, first, on the other machine.
  • To check that SAT is at the far end, start a gRPC listener first, on the other machine: in SAT open Tools > Network Tools, choose gRPC listener, set Listen port to the port the test uses and Duration seconds to cover it, and choose Listen for gRPC transport. Accept multiple connections until timeout starts ticked, so a second test can follow. Run gRPC connectivity from this machine afterwards.
  • To let the test reach the listener, allow the port towards the machine with the listener in every firewall between the two machines, and allow SAT when Windows asks whether it may listen on the network, first, on that machine. The answer stays as a firewall rule.
To test gRPC transport to a host, do the following:
  1. In Customer / Lab, open Tools > Network Tools and choose gRPC Connectivity.
  2. Fill in the fields. The table below describes each.
  3. Choose Test gRPC transport.

With TLS the results show the certificate the server presented: subject, issuer, validity and SHA-256. When the peer answers with something that is not HTTP/2, a First bytes row shows what it sent and what it looks like: an HTTP/1.x response, a TLS record, an SSH banner, or binary data such as Veeam's own transport. Veeam's data ports (2500 to 3300, 6162) speak that transport, so the test stops there at the SETTINGS stage; the Veeam Service Channel tests the channel Veeam's own processes use.

FieldWhat it does
Target hostRequired. The host that serves the gRPC or HTTP/2 transport: its name or IP address.
PortRequired. The port the service listens on. Starts as 2500.
TLS server name / SNI (optional)Optional. The TLS server name presented when Use TLS and require ALPN h2 is ticked. Empty uses Target host.
Use TLS and require ALPN h2Optional. Ticked, the connection uses TLS and the server has to offer ALPN h2. Clear to begin with, when the HTTP/2 preface is sent over plain TCP.

gRPC Listener

gRPC Listener runs SAT's HTTP/2 and gRPC listener on this machine, so gRPC Connectivity on another machine has a known far end.

Before You Begin

  • Windows can ask whether to allow SAT to listen on the network the first time: allow it for the network the other machine connects over. The answer stays as a firewall rule.

  1. On the destination, start gRPC Listener on port 2500 or another approved free port.
  2. On the source, run gRPC Connectivity against that destination and port.
  3. Use TLS only when the endpoint is expected to negotiate TLS/ALPN.
  4. Compare the SAT peer verification/Test ID in both results.
Expected result. The result covers the TCP and HTTP/2 transport path between the two machines and names the layer where gRPC transport fails. An application's own gRPC methods are not called.

Tools > Network Tools > Veeam Service Channel

Veeam Service Channel

Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows' tray, jobs and control panel reach the Veeam service over gRPC on a named pipe on the same machine. The Veeam Service Channel tests that channel in layers and stops at the first that fails. Choose the Veeam product; Log folder reads another folder of the product's logs, such as a collected bundle's, and Read the logs only skips the live layers.

Before you start

  • To test the channel the way the Agent reaches it, start SAT first on the computer that runs the Veeam service, as the user who sees the error. The service, its pipe and the HTTP/2 handshake on the pipe are tested from this machine as the account running SAT.
  • To read a collected bundle's logs in place of this machine's, name the folder of the product's logs in Log folder and tick Read the logs only first.
LayerWhat it shows
ServiceThe Veeam service that hosts the gRPC server: running or not, start type, account, process and when it started.
Named pipeWhether the service's named pipe is present, by its known name.
HTTP/2 handshakeAn HTTP/2 handshake on the pipe as the account running SAT: the server's SETTINGS and a PING answered. No gRPC call is made; SAT closes with GOAWAY.
LogsThe gRPC lines the product logged in the hours chosen: service starts and stops, clients that could not connect (KB2127), calls whose deadline passed, with the call named, and teardown noise from the service's gRPC host.

The summary is one sentence for the case note, such as: the service is running, its pipe accepts this account and speaks HTTP/2, and the product logged no gRPC errors in the last 24 hours. For Veeam Backup & Replication the service and its logs are read; its pipe is not known yet.

To test the Veeam Service Channel, do the following:
  1. Start SAT on the computer that runs the Veeam service, as the user who sees the error.
  2. Open Tools > Network Tools in the Customer / Lab role and choose Veeam Service Channel.
  3. In Veeam product, choose agent for Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows, or vbr for Veeam Backup & Replication.
  4. To read a collected bundle's logs, choose its folder in Log folder and tick Read the logs only. Leave Log folder empty to read the product's own folder.
  5. In Hours, set how far back the logs are read. The default is 24.
  6. Choose Test channel. The table lists each layer with its check, details and status, and stops at the first layer that fails.
FieldWhat it does
Veeam productOptional. The product whose channel is tested: agent for Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows, or vbr for Veeam Backup & Replication. Empty uses agent.
HoursOptional. How far back the logs are read, in hours. Empty, or a value that is not a positive number, uses 24.
Log folderOptional. A folder of the product's logs, such as a collected bundle's Endpoint folder. Empty reads the product's own log folder on this machine.
Read the logs onlyOptional. Ticked, the service, its named pipe and the HTTP/2 handshake on this machine are skipped and only the product's logs are read. Clear to begin with.

Tools > Network Tools > SMB Connectivity

SMB Connectivity

Use this tool to independently validate Windows SMB access to a target. The default bounded test path is \\targetmachine\C$\Windows\Veeam. SAT verifies TCP/445, establishes or observes the SMB session, reports negotiated SMB details when Windows exposes them, accesses the target path, creates a uniquely named small SAT payload, reads/verifies it, deletes it, and reports cleanup status.

Before you start

  • To use SMB connectivity test, have the target's name or address and an account that is an administrator of it first: the test path is under C$, which only administrators of the target can open.
  • To connect as another account, tick Prompt Windows for alternate credentials and Windows asks for it. Without it the test connects as the account SAT runs as. Windows keeps one set of credentials for each server, so close an existing connection to the target made with other credentials first.
  • To run the write, read and delete test, name an existing folder under C$ in Bounded test path (C$\Windows\Veeam to begin with) first, on the target. The account needs write access to the folder.
  • To reach the target, open TCP 445 from this machine to it through every firewall between them first.
Credential handling. An alternate SMB password is not stored. Current-identity mode uses the caller's Windows token. Alternate-credential mode delegates the interactive credential prompt to Windows and uses a temporary deviceless SMB connection; the password is not written into SAT command lines, case data, diagnostic artifacts, configuration, or debug output.
To test SMB safely, do the following:
  1. Enter the target machine and bounded share path.
  2. Choose the current Windows identity or request the Windows-owned alternate-credential prompt.
  3. Run the test and review TCP/445, SMB session/dialect, path-access, payload verification and cleanup stages.
  4. If SAT created a temporary SMB session, confirm that session cleanup reports success.
Result. The diagnostic distinguishes basic TCP reachability from SMB negotiation, authentication/path access, write/read verification and cleanup so an SMB-related case symptom can be compared with behavior outside Veeam.
FieldWhat it does
Target machineRequired. The Windows computer to test: its host name, fully qualified name or IPv4 address.
Bounded test pathRequired. A folder under C$ on the target, written as C$ followed by the folder. The test writes a small file there, reads it back and deletes it, so the account needs write access. Starts as C$\Windows\Veeam.
TCP / SMB timeout msRequired. How long to wait at each SMB stage, in milliseconds. Starts as 5000.
Prompt Windows for alternate credentialsOptional. Ticked, Windows asks for the account to connect with. Clear to begin with, when the test connects as the account SAT runs as.

Tools > Network Tools > TCP / UDP Listener

TCP / UDP Listener

Use the listener on a second customer/lab host when you need to verify that a test packet or connection reaches that system. The listener records controlled endpoint information and SAT Test IDs into SAT-owned tool output so the result can later be included in Universal Log Collection.

The first time SAT listens on a network, Windows can ask whether to allow SupportAssistTool.exe, and the answer stays on the machine as a firewall rule. The listener says so when it starts, and when it stops it lists the firewall rules that name SAT (FIREWALL rows) so they can be removed in Windows Defender Firewall once the test is done.

Before you start

  • To receive a test, start the listener first, on the machine that receives it, before the test begins on the other machine. That machine tests this machine's address and the Listen port.
  • To keep the listener open for the whole test, set Duration seconds to cover it. The listener stops when that time ends, and a TCP listener stops after its first connection unless Accept multiple connections until timeout is ticked.
  • To verify a UDP listener, choose UDP connectivity test on the other machine, tick Verify a cooperating SAT UDP listener there and test this machine's address.
  • To let the test reach the listener, allow the Listen port towards the machine with the listener in every firewall between the two machines.
  • To let the listener accept connections, allow SAT when Windows asks whether it may listen on the network, first, on the machine with the listener. Allow it for the network the other machine connects over.
To verify a path between two SAT hosts, do the following:
  1. On the destination host, enable Customer / Lab mode and open TCP / UDP Listener.
  2. Select TCP or UDP and the test port, optionally configure a TCP banner, then start the listener.
  3. Keep the listener page open: accepted connections and SAT verification details appear live as traffic is received; you do not need to stop the listener to see them.
  4. On the source host, open Remote Port Checker and target the listener.
  5. Enable SAT-to-SAT verification where applicable and run the test.
  6. Compare the Test ID shown on both systems. For TCP, you can also enable in-memory payload validation and review the banner sent/received state.
Result. Both SAT instances retain a correlated result showing the observed endpoints, protocol, time, SAT acknowledgement, and applicable banner/payload state. Generic non-SAT connections are logged as connection events without reading arbitrary application payloads.

If the listener belongs to a case or No Case session group, switching the Active case hides the tab without stopping the listener. See Case-Scoped Tool Sessions.

TCP listener.

FieldWhat it does
Listen portRequired. The TCP port this machine accepts connections on. Starts as 2500.
Duration secondsRequired. How long the listener stays open. Starts as 30.
BannerOptional. Text sent to each client that connects, so the other end can confirm it reached this listener. %port% is replaced by the listen port. Empty sends no banner.
Accept multiple connections until timeoutOptional. Ticked, the listener keeps accepting connections until Duration seconds ends. Clear to begin with, when it stops after the first connection.

UDP listener.

FieldWhat it does

Duration secondsRequired. How long the listener stays open. Starts as 30.

Tools > Network Tools > Local Loopback Self-Test

Local Loopback Self-Test

Use Local Loopback Self-Test to confirm that the local SAT/socket protocol path works before blaming a remote network path. Loopback is a local self-test and is not proof that two separate systems can communicate.

To run a safe loopback test, do the following:
  1. Select the global IPv4 and/or IPv6 address-family mode.
  2. Enter the test port; SAT defaults to 2500.
  3. Run the test.
  4. SAT first checks whether the requested port is already bound/listening. If another SAT listener, service, or application owns the port, SAT reports that condition and does not attempt to create a competing listener.
  5. If the port is free, SAT starts its temporary listener, waits for the listener-ready state, performs the loopback exchange, then stops only the temporary listener it created.
Result. A passing loopback test confirms the local socket/SAT path. Compare it with a two-endpoint test when diagnosing remote connectivity.
FieldWhat it does
Loopback portRequired. The port the temporary listener uses, on this machine only. When another program already owns the port, the test names the owner and does not start. Starts as 2500.
Timeout msRequired. How long to wait for the temporary listener to start and for the local connection, in milliseconds. Starts as 5000.

Tools > Network Tools > Packet Capture

Packet Capture

Packet Capture records this machine's network traffic with Packet Monitor (pktmon), the capture built into Windows, or with netsh trace when pktmon is missing or does not start, and converts it to PCAPNG for Wireshark. Open Tools > Network Tools in the Customer / Lab role and choose Packet capture. Start capture begins the capture, and the same button reads Stop capture while it runs. IP filter and Port filter narrow the capture to one address or one port. The capture is saved as Packet-Capture.etl in this run's tool output.

Before you start

  • To capture, start SAT as administrator, or approve the administrator prompt when you choose Start capture. One approval covers Start capture and Stop capture.
  • To capture the traffic that matters, start the capture first, on the machine whose traffic is wanted, before the problem is reproduced. IP filter and Port filter are optional.
  • To finish, choose Stop capture, the same button. The capture is converted to PCAPNG and its notable events are listed. Closing SAT with a capture running asks what to do with it.

What the result shows

While the capture runs, a Packets so far row counts the packets and is refreshed every 5 seconds. After Stop capture, the PCAPNG file is written with the pktmon converter, and with etl2pcapng only when pktmon cannot read the capture. The notable events of the capture are listed with their times: TCP retransmissions, duplicate acknowledgements, resets, zero windows, missing segments and TLS alerts. Copies of one packet logged at several pktmon components count once.

The command-line twins are packet start, packet status, packet stop, packet convert and packet events.

To capture network traffic, do the following:
  1. Open Tools > Network Tools in the Customer / Lab role and choose Packet capture.
  2. To narrow the capture, type an address in IP filter and a port in Port filter.
  3. Choose Start capture and approve the administrator prompt. A Packets so far row counts the packets every 5 seconds.
  4. Reproduce the problem.
  5. Choose Stop capture. The capture is converted to PCAPNG and its notable events are listed.
  6. Open the PCAPNG file from this run's tool output in Wireshark to read it.
FieldWhat it does
IP filterOptional. Limits the capture to traffic to or from one IP address. Empty captures every address.
Port filterOptional. Limits the capture to one port, entered as a number. Empty captures every port.

Tools > Network Tools > Network Throughput

Network Throughput

Use the native SAT throughput client/server when you need a longer sustained data-rate test between two customer/lab hosts. This is separate from the bounded in-memory payload validation: payload validation answers whether a controlled application-sized transfer completes intact; throughput testing measures sustained transfer behavior over a selected interval/amount.

Network Tools also has iPerf client (optional) and iPerf one-shot server (optional), which run an iPerf3 copy that is already on the machine for a measurement with iPerf3 on both ends. Server address, Port and Transfer size set the client's run, and Optional tools folder names the folder that holds iperf3.

Before you start

Native throughput

  • To receive the data, start Native throughput server first, on the receiving machine: set Listen port to the port the client will use and choose Start server. It waits for the client for the time in Connection timeout ms, 60 seconds to begin with.
  • To send it, run Native throughput client on the sending machine with the receiving machine's address and the same port, before that time ends. The test loads the network between the two machines while it runs.
  • To let the client reach the server, allow the port towards the receiving machine in every firewall between the two machines, and allow SAT when Windows asks whether it may listen on the network, first, on the receiving machine. The answer stays as a firewall rule.

iPerf3 (optional)

  • To use iPerf client (optional) or iPerf one-shot server (optional), have iPerf3 on both machines first: get it on the Integrations page, or name the folder that holds it in Optional tools folder.
  • To measure, start iPerf one-shot server (optional) first, on the receiving machine, then run iPerf client (optional) on the other machine with the same Port. The server takes a single run.
  • To let the client reach the server, allow iPerf3 when Windows asks whether it may listen on the network, first, on the machine with the server. Allow it for the network the other machine connects over.
To run a SAT-to-SAT throughput test, do the following:
  1. On the destination host, choose Native throughput server in Network Tools and start it.
  2. On the source host, choose Native throughput client.
  3. Enter the destination host/port and configured test settings.
  4. Run the client and review transferred bytes, elapsed time, and measured rate on completion.
Result. Both hosts retain SAT-owned diagnostic output that can be included in Universal Log Collection.

Tools > SQL Tools

SQL Tools

SQL Tools checks a SQL Server or PostgreSQL server against Veeam's guides: an account's permissions, the shape of the server, the backup history and log chain, the database files and a query of your own. Use it when a Veeam job cannot reach its database, a log backup fails, or the configuration database needs to be identified. SQL Server is read over ODBC and PostgreSQL through psql.

Before you start

  • To check an instance, have its name as clients connect to it first, such as SQLHOST01\VEEAMSQL2016.
  • To check SQL Server, install Microsoft's ODBC Driver 18 or 17 for SQL Server first, on the machine SAT runs on. The older SQL Server driver in Windows is tried after the two ODBC drivers.
  • To check PostgreSQL, set Engine to PostgreSQL and make psql available first: place it in the Tools folder on the Integrations page, or install the PostgreSQL client tools.
  • To connect as the account whose access is in question, start SAT as that account with Use logged-in user ticked. Clear it to be asked for a SQL login, which is used for that run and not saved.
  • To check the account Veeam uses with Permission check, start SAT as that account first. Another account is looked up in the catalog and needs VIEW ANY DEFINITION or sysadmin for the account connecting; its Windows groups are not expanded.
  • To see each file's volume (kind, bus, file system and sector size) in Database files and volumes, run SAT on the SQL host first.

Each operation connects to the server chosen from this machine's instances or the configuration database's server, or typed. Use logged-in user connects as the account running SAT and counts its Windows groups as SQL Server does; to check the account Veeam uses, run SAT as that account. Clear it to be asked for a login, which is used for that run and not saved. Trust the server certificate accepts SQL Server's own self-signed certificate. Another account reads that login's catalog rows instead, which needs VIEW ANY DEFINITION and does not expand its groups. Every check reads only. A row's status is Pass, Attention, Fail, Not applicable, Could not check or Info, and a comparison names the Veeam page it follows.

Engine is the last field of every operation: SQL Server or PostgreSQL. The server field lists this machine's SQL Server instances and PostgreSQL servers, each marked with its engine, and choosing one sets Engine. A server typed in the field leaves Engine as it was chosen. Changing the engine also changes the Database and Query fields from one engine's starting value to the other's, where they still hold it.

Show CLI on SQL Tools shows the command with --show-sql, which prints the SQL the check runs, and under the command the SQL itself, headed by the engine: SQL Server or PostgreSQL. For a Read-only query the command carries that engine's statement in --query, on one line, so a named query shows the SQL it runs for the chosen engine.

The Database and Configuration database fields list the databases the server accepts connections to when their list is opened. The list is read as the account running SAT, so it needs Use logged-in user. It is kept for the session, so opening it again is immediate, and a name can always be typed. When the server cannot be read, the status line says why and the list stays as it was.

Running the checks

To run a check, do the following:
  1. Open Tools > SQL Tools and choose the card: Permission check, Server shape, Backups and log chain or Database files.
  2. In SQL Server / instance, choose one of this machine's instances from the list, or type the server name as clients connect to it. Choosing a listed instance sets Engine.
  3. Leave Use logged-in user ticked to connect as the account running SAT. Clear it to be asked for a SQL login. Tick Trust the server certificate when the server presents a certificate this machine does not trust.
  4. Fill the fields the check has: Check against, Configuration database and Another account for the Permission check, and Database and Days for Backups and log chain. Days is 14 when left alone.
  5. Choose Run check, Read shape, Read backups or Read files. The table lists each check with its status, and the result line counts them.

PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL runs through psql, which SAT finds in the Tools folder, on the PATH or in the PostgreSQL install folders. Place psql in the Tools folder from Integrations, or use the one installed with PostgreSQL. Tools > VSS Tools

VSS Tools

VSS Tools is an isolated diagnostic area for enumerating VSS writers and running a controlled SAT-owned VSS test workflow. The main SAT process remains non-elevated and routes native VSS requester operations through the authenticated elevated helper after Windows administrator approval. Snapshot tests select from the detected applicable NTFS/ReFS volumes, stream the participating writer identities and states while the test runs, and keep the cleanup-verification evidence so you can show the snapshot was released.

Before you start

  • To enumerate the writers, run Enumerate VSS Writers on the machine whose snapshots fail first. Reading the writers needs administrator rights: Windows asks for approval once.
  • To run the test snapshot, run Create / hold / release test snapshot on the machine whose snapshots fail first. The test takes a temporary shadow copy of each volume entered, holds it for the seconds given and releases it, then checks that it is gone. It runs in the privileged helper, so Windows asks for administrator approval.

Related topics

Reviewing Source EvidenceTroubleshooting

Enumerate VSS Writers

List writer identities, current state, and last reported failure information. Requests elevation when required, authenticates the helper, and reports writer-enumeration state.

Before You Begin

  • Run it on the machine whose snapshots fail. Reading the writers needs administrator rights: Windows asks for approval once.
To list the VSS writers and their state, do the following:
  1. In Customer / Lab, open Tools > VSS Tools and choose Enumerate VSS Writers.
  2. Choose Refresh writers.

Related topics

VSS Tools
Tools > VSS Tools > Run VSS Test Job

Run VSS Test Job

Create, hold, complete, and release a SAT-owned test snapshot set using the selected options. Streams elevation, requester phases, snapshot-created state, hold countdown, backup completion, delete, and cleanup-verification stages.

Before You Begin

  • Run it on the machine whose snapshots fail. The test takes a temporary shadow copy of each volume entered, holds it for the seconds given and releases it, then checks that it is gone.
  • The test runs in the privileged helper, so Windows asks for administrator approval.
To run and verify a VSS test snapshot, do the following:
  1. Open VSS Tools and select Create / hold / release test snapshot.
  2. Choose an applicable local volume from the VSS-capable volume dropdown. SAT prefers drive letters/mount paths and falls back to the Volume GUID when no drive letter is assigned. Set the hold duration and any writer/component options required for the diagnostic.
  3. Choose Run. If Windows requires administrator rights, approve the UAC request. If approval is declined, SAT stops before VSS initialization.
  4. Watch the results list while SAT initializes the requester and creates the snapshot. Participating VSS writers are shown with state and class/instance identity as they are observed. During the hold period, the SAT-owned snapshot remains marked active and the countdown updates.
  5. When the hold ends (or Cancel is requested), SAT completes/marks the requester state, deletes only its own snapshot set, and performs a short verification window against the exact snapshot IDs it created.
  6. Review the terminal state. CLEANUP VERIFIED means those SAT-owned snapshot IDs remained absent through the verification passes. A cleanup warning means deletion/verification requires review; it does not authorize SAT to delete unrelated snapshots.
Result. The operation has an explicit lifecycle from elevation through cleanup.

After the delete phase, SAT verifies cleanup of the SAT-created snapshot by checking the exact snapshot identifiers created by the test. A cleanup warning means the engineer should review the reported state; Unrelated snapshots are not removed.

Use only as a controlled diagnostic. The VSS test creates real VSS operations on the local execution host. Review the selected volumes and options before running it. SAT runs stateful VSS Lab operations one at a time, even if more than one copy of SAT is open, and cleans up only the snapshot set it created.

For a test that names writers, Choose... beside Writer class GUIDs lists the writers the last Enumerate VSS Writers run found, such as SQL Server or Active Directory, as a checked list. The ticked ones fill the field; ids already typed come ticked. Run Enumerate VSS Writers first.

FieldWhat it does
VSS-capable volumeRequired. The local NTFS or ReFS volume to take a temporary shadow copy of, such as C:\. Several volumes can be separated by semicolons.
Writer class GUIDs (optional)Optional. The VSS writers to include in the snapshot, by writer class GUID, separated by semicolons. Choose lists them. Empty includes every writer.
Hold secondsRequired. How long the shadow copy is held before it is released and checked for cleanup. Starts as 30.
Full backup stateOptional. Ticked, the test snapshot takes a full backup state. Cleared, it takes a copy backup state, which leaves the writers' backup history as it was. Clear to begin with.
Select all selectable writer componentsOptional. Ticked, the snapshot runs in component mode with every selectable writer component selected. Clear to begin with.

Tools > System Differences

System Differences

System Differences shows what changed on this machine between two moments: capture what is there, make the change or wait for it, then compare. The page has a card for each type, File Differences and Registry Differences. Each card opens one page holding all of that type's fields and three buttons: Capture on the left, Compare and Open.

Before you start

  • To capture files, choose the folder in Folder to look at and a file in Capture file first. A capture file holds one capture, so capturing to an existing file replaces it after a question.
  • To read the folder from the NTFS master file table and record where the NTFS change journal stood, start SAT as administrator before the capture. Without it the folder is read folder by folder, and places that need administrator rights are listed as Skipped.
  • To compare what the change did, make the change after the capture finishes, then choose Compare.
  • To compare with Now, keep the folder where it was captured, as Now reads the folder again with the capture's own settings and in the way the capture read it. A second capture file in Compare with compares the two captures instead.
  • To read the NTFS change journal during a compare, start SAT as administrator for the compare as well. The result line says when the journal was not read.
To read what a capture holds, do the following:
  1. Open the File Differences card, or the Registry Differences card for a registry capture.
  2. Choose the capture in Capture file.
  3. Choose Open. The list shows what the capture file holds, and the result line gives the totals and how many compares are kept in it.

The first rows of a files capture are Capture, with what it covers, when and on which machine it was taken and the object count; Taken as, administrator or standard user, and the system; Read from, the NTFS master file table or folder by folder; Skipped places; Compare file contents; and Change journal. The compares kept in the file follow, newest first: a Compare row with what it was compared with, when, and its counts, then its rows. Then each file and folder of the capture, in path order, with its size, last write time and, when contents were read, its SHA-256. A registry capture lists its compares the same way, then each key with its view and last write time and its values with their data. The first 100,000 are listed, and the result line gives the totals. Open only reads the capture file.

FieldWhat it does
Folder to look atEverything under this folder is captured.
Capture fileThe .satsnap file Capture writes and Compare and Open read. A capture file holds one capture; capturing to an existing file asks before replacing it. Each compare is kept in it.
Compare file contentsNever compares names, sizes and times. Files up to 64 MB and All files also read each file.
Include alternate data streamsRecords each file's alternate data streams as well. A capture with streams is read folder by folder.
Registry scopeThe registry key the capture starts from, or a whole hive: HKLM, HKU, HKCR, HKCC or HKCU.
Registry viewboth, 64 or 32.
Compare withNow, or a second capture file.

As administrator, for a folder on a local NTFS volume, Capture reads the folder from the volume's master file table, where NTFS keeps each file's name, folder, times, size and attributes. The table is read through NTFS itself. A plain file's details come from the table; a folder, a link and a file whose contents are read are opened one by one, as folder by folder. On another file system, without administrator, or when the table cannot be read, the folder is read folder by folder, and the result line says why. Compare with Now reads this machine the way the capture was read. When it cannot, as for a capture read from the table compared without administrator, the result line says so, as sizes on disk and folders SAT could not open can then differ for that reason alone.

A capture records one moment. A capture taken as administrator also records where the NTFS change journal stood, and a compare run as administrator reads the journal from there. It adds a created-and-deleted row for each file created and removed in between, with the times, and a renamed row for each file renamed, which two captures alone cannot show, and the result line counts what the journal recorded under the folder. A capture taken without administrator records no journal position, and the result line says the journal was not read. Windows keeps a limited journal, so after a long time or much activity the part covering the capture may be overwritten, which the result line also says.

Cancel stops a capture or a compare at once. A compare of a large folder finishes in seconds or minutes. Read folder by folder, a capture reads each folder's entries in one call; a file's hard-link count is not read that way, and a compare does not count an unread count as a change. A cancelled capture is not kept, as it cannot be compared. Last-access time alone is not a difference, as reading a file changes it. A whole volume takes far longer than a folder, and its capture file can reach several gigabytes; Compare with Now writes a temporary capture of about the same size to this machine's temporary folder and removes it afterwards.

The command line runs the same operations: files baseline, then files compare with --live or --other, and registry baseline and registry compare for the registry. --keep keeps the compare in the capture file, as the page does, and baseline inspect --file lists a capture, how it was read and its kept compares. Show CLI prints the command for the form; for Open it is baseline inspect --file <file>.

Related topics

Tools OverviewLast Tool Output
Tools > System Differences > File Differences

File Differences

File Differences records a folder's files and folders as they are now, then compares that capture with the folder later or with a second capture, so what changed in between is listed.

Before You Begin

  • Choose the folder to capture and a file name in Save capture as. A capture file holds one capture, so an existing file is replaced after a question.
  • Make the change after the capture finishes, then choose Compare.
  • Run SAT as administrator. Places that need administrator rights are listed as Skipped without it, and the capture also records where the NTFS change journal stood, which lets the compare list files created and removed in between.
  • Have the capture file from Capture, and make the change before comparing.
  • Compare with Now reads the folder again with the same settings, so the folder has to be where it was captured. A second capture file compares the two captures instead.
  • Run SAT as administrator for the compare as well. Reading the NTFS change journal needs it, and the result line says when it was not read.
To find what changed, do the following:
  1. Open the File Differences card. In Folder to look at choose the folder, such as C:\ProgramData\Veeam. Capture file fills with a file in this run's tool output when Capture is chosen; choose another file to keep it elsewhere.
  2. Leave Compare file contents at Never, or choose Files up to 64 MB or All files to find a change that left a file's size and times alone. Reading contents takes longer.
  3. Choose Capture. The result line says how many objects were captured, how long it took, whether the folder was read from the NTFS master file table or folder by folder, and how many places were skipped because they need administrator rights.
  4. Make the change, or wait for it.
  5. Leave Compare with at Now to read the folder again, or choose a second capture file.
  6. Choose Compare. The result line counts what was added, removed, changed, and moved or renamed, and says when and where the capture was taken. Each row gives the reason and the values before and after. The compare is kept in the capture file.

Without administrator rights, Capture asks whether to capture as administrator. Yes shows the Windows approval prompt, and the capture reads the folder from the NTFS master file table and records where the change journal stands. No, or declining the prompt, captures folder by folder. Compare with Now of a capture read from the master file table asks whether to read this machine as administrator, and Yes and No work the same way. The result line, and the Read from row of Open, say how the folder was read.

When the capture file is not there yet, Compare takes the capture first and then compares it with Now.

To compare two captures, do the following:
  1. Capture the folder to a first file with Capture, make the change, then choose a second file in Capture file and choose Capture again.
  2. Choose the first file in Capture file.
  3. In Compare with, choose the second capture file.
  4. Choose Compare. The result line counts what was added, removed, changed, and moved or renamed between the two captures.
FieldWhat it does
Compare file contentsOptional. Never compares names, sizes and times. Files up to 64 MB and All files also read each file, which finds a change that left its size and times alone. Empty is read as Never.
Folder to look atRequired. Everything under this folder is captured. Capture needs it; Compare reads the folder again from the capture's own settings.
Capture fileRequired. The .satsnap file Capture writes (an existing one is replaced after a question) and Compare and Open read; Compare captures first when it is not there yet. Compares are kept in it.
Compare withOptional. Now reads the folder again with the capture's settings and compares; a second .satsnap capture compares the two captures. Empty is read as Now.
Include alternate data streamsOptional. Ticked, Capture also records each file's alternate data streams. Clear to begin with.

Registry viewOptional. both, 64 or 32: the 64-bit view, the 32-bit view or both. Empty is read as both.
Capture fileRequired. The .satsnap file Capture writes (an existing one is replaced after a question) and Compare and Open read; Compare captures first when it is not there yet. Compares are kept in it.

Tools > WMI Diagnostics

WMI Diagnostics

WMI Diagnostics reads Windows Management Instrumentation. WMI Health checks this machine; the other tools read this machine or another one. Veeam reads much of what it knows about a Windows host through WMI, so a WMI fault shows up in Veeam as a failed inventory, a failed guest operation or a missing volume. Open Tools > WMI Diagnostics in the Customer / Lab role and choose a card. Every tool here only reads.

WMI Health: The machine, the WMI service and the services it needs, the repository, a timed probe of each namespace Veeam reads, and the WMI faults Windows logged. See WMI Health.

Process Inventory is on Host Diagnostics and lists this machine's processes. See Host Diagnostics.

A query to another machine shows its stages as rows while it runs: Connect, Query and Read rows. The row of the stage that fails names the machine and the WMI error with its meaning.

WMI Cluster Diagnostics and Custom WMI Query take Machine: a dot for this machine, or another machine's name or address. Choose... lists this machine first, then the active case's machines and the addresses saved in Settings. Another machine is read over DCOM: TCP 135 and then a dynamic RPC port. Sign in chooses the account used on another machine: Current Windows account is the account SAT runs as, and Another account asks for an account and its password when you choose Query. A machine that refuses the account, or a firewall that blocks the ports, fails the connection, and the result names the WMI error and what it means.

Signing in to another machine

Use Another account when the account SAT runs as is not allowed on the other machine, such as a lab machine in a workgroup or a server in another domain. The account and password are used for that one query and are not saved. With another account the connection is encrypted (packet privacy). This machine always uses the account SAT runs as.

To query another machine as another account, do the following:

  1. Open Tools > WMI Diagnostics and choose WMI Cluster Diagnostics or Custom WMI Query.
  2. In Machine, type the other machine's name or address.
  3. In Sign in, choose Another account.
  4. Choose Query.
  5. In the Windows sign-in dialog, type the account as DOMAIN\name, as name@domain, or as a name alone for an account of that machine, and its password. Then choose OK.

A wrong account or password reads E_ACCESSDENIED: DCOM refused the account. Show CLI writes the command with --user ACCOUNT; the command line reads the password from the SAT_WMI_PASSWORD environment variable.

Before you start

The list for WMI Health is in its own article, WMI Health.

  • WMI Cluster Diagnostics. To read a cluster, run it on a cluster node, or name one in Machine, first. A machine without the failover cluster role reads NOT CLUSTERED. Use an account that administers the cluster: start SAT as that account, or choose it in Sign in. A node on another machine is reached over DCOM, so TCP 135 and the dynamic RPC ports have to be open from this machine to it.
  • Custom WMI Query. To query another machine, name it in Machine and use an account that WMI on that machine allows, usually an administrator of it: the account SAT runs as, or the one Sign in asks for. It is reached over DCOM (TCP 135 and the dynamic RPC ports). To run the shadow storage and shadow copy examples, or to query BitLocker's namespace, start SAT as administrator first.

The command-line twins are wmi query --preset host|cluster, wmi query --namespace ... --query ... and wmi health. wmi query --machine HOST --user ACCOUNT signs in as another account.

Tools > WMI Diagnostics > WMI Health

WMI Health

WMI health checks Windows Management Instrumentation on this machine in five stages, and lists the results as a table of Stage, Finding, Detail and Status. The check only reads. Open Tools > WMI Diagnostics in the Customer / Lab role and choose the operation WMI health, or its card, then choose Check. It has no fields; to check another machine's WMI, run SAT on that machine.

Before you start

  • To check a machine's WMI, run SAT on that machine. To include the Repository stage, start SAT as administrator first.
StageWhat it checks
HostThe machine's name, its Windows (edition, version, build and architecture) and when it last started, read through WMI. A machine WMI does not answer for fails here first.
ServiceThe Winmgmt service's state and start type, then each service Winmgmt depends on, as Windows lists them. A service that is stopped or disabled is a finding.
RepositoryRuns winmgmt /verifyrepository and shows its exit code with its own text: 0 is consistent, any other exit code is a finding. Then adds up the files in %windir%\System32\wbem\Repository against the 4 GB limit; 90% or more is a finding.
NamespacesConnects to each namespace Veeam reads and runs one small query, timed: root\cimv2, root\wmi, root\StandardCimv2, root\Microsoft\Windows\Storage, Hyper-V's root\virtualization\v2, Failover Clustering's root\MSCluster and BitLocker's root\CIMV2\Security\MicrosoftVolumeEncryption. An answer slower than 2 seconds is a finding. A namespace the machine does not have reads Not present, with the role or feature it belongs to.
Recent faultsReads the last 7 days of event 5858 from the Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational log, a WMI operation that failed, grouped by its ResultCode: each group gives the count, the newest time, what the code means and the newest message. Also event 5612 from the Application log, a provider host that WMI stopped for a quota. The events from this run's own namespace probes are left out and counted.

Status

StatusMeaning
PassThe item was checked and is as expected.
FindingThe item needs a look: a stopped or disabled service, an inconsistent or nearly full repository, a slow or failing namespace, or WMI faults in the period.
Not presentThe namespace or log is not on the machine, usually because its role or feature is not installed.
Needs administratorThe account SAT runs as was refused. Run SAT as administrator, or with an account allowed on the other machine, to include it.

What needs administrator

The repository check runs only when SAT runs as administrator; otherwise its row reads Needs administrator and the other stages run as usual. Start SAT as administrator to include it. A namespace that refuses the account also reads Needs administrator: BitLocker's namespace does for a standard user.

An inconsistent repository

WMI health verifies the repository and changes nothing. When winmgmt /verifyrepository finds it inconsistent, the finding names what Microsoft documents for that: winmgmt /salvagerepository, then winmgmt /resetrepository. Run them yourself, from an elevated prompt, after reading Microsoft's guidance for them.

Another machine

The command-line twin is wmi health; it exits 3 when a row is a finding. Its --machine option checks another machine's service and namespaces over DCOM, as the command-line guide describes.

To check WMI on this machine, do the following:
  1. Open Tools > WMI Diagnostics in the Customer / Lab role and choose WMI Health. The form has no fields: the check reads this machine.
  2. Choose Check. The table lists each stage with its finding, detail and status.
  3. Select a row to read its whole text in the pane under the table.
  4. To check another machine, use WMI Cluster Diagnostics or Custom WMI Query and choose the machine in Machine. See WMI Diagnostics.

Tools > VBR Diagnostics > Running VBR Jobs

Running VBR Jobs

Use this Windows/VBR-server tool to review active VBR job sessions through the locally installed Veeam Backup PowerShell module. SAT exposes this tool only after positive local VBR installation detection; the shared Veeam Backup log directory alone does not satisfy that check. SAT normalizes supported backup/replication, backup copy, Agent, tape, SureBackup and application-backup work into one active-session list. Session families with no documented safe stop mapping remain visible as read-only.

Before you start

  • To list the jobs, run Running VBR Jobs on the backup server first: the list is read through the local Veeam PowerShell module.
  • To read the list, start SAT as a Windows account that has a role in the backup server's Users and Roles, as for the Veeam console. No administrator rights are needed.
Column / actionPurpose
Job NameDisplayed job or active-session identity. Sort by the column header.
TypeNormalized job/session family.
Started / ProgressObserved start time and progress information where the Veeam PowerShell object provides it. Sort by the column header; start defaults newest-first.
State / ActionObserved active state plus stop-request state.
Copy DetailsCopy the normalized full row record. Right-click the row or press Ctrl+C.
Stop selectedAfter confirmation, send the supported Veeam stop command for that job/session family. The row stays until a refresh confirms the session ended.
RefreshRe-query active VBR sessions. A successfully stopped session is confirmed only when it is absent from the active inventory.
To stop an active job safely, do the following:
  1. Run Running VBR Jobs on the VBR server and select the active row.
  2. Review/copy the session details if required for the case.
  3. Select Stop selected and confirm the one-time stop request.
  4. SAT changes that row to STOP REQUESTED and disables another stop request for the same displayed session.
  5. Select Refresh. If the active session is gone, the stop is confirmed. If it remains, SAT continues to show its current reported state for follow-up.
Result. The action requests that the current active run stop; it does not disable the configured job schedule or claim completion before a refresh confirms the session is not active.
Local execution and PowerShell host. Running VBR Jobs uses the Veeam Backup PowerShell module on the local VBR server with the current Windows identity. SAT uses PowerShell 7/pwsh.exe when required by the installed Veeam module and can use the compatible local Windows PowerShell host for older modules. Remote PowerShell credentials are not persisted, and no remote administrative session is created for this tool.

Tools Overview
Tools > Host Diagnostics

Host Diagnostics

Host Diagnostics checks this machine: its clock, open files, volumes, Veeam's services and processes, the usual causes of a failed snapshot or backup, its processes and named pipes, and the Windows Installer cache. The page groups its tools in three sections.

Quick checks

  • Time Check (F7): This clock against its time source, and a timestamp converter.
  • File Lock Check (F8): Which process holds a file open, or anything under a folder.
  • Volume Check (F9): Every volume, what it sits on, and whether Fast Clone can work there.
  • Service and Process Watch (F12): Veeam's services and processes as they start, stop and end, with their ports.

Host checks

  • Host Checks: Read-only checks of what most often explains a failed snapshot or backup: backup events, the Veeam drivers, VSS shadow storage, and the .NET and TLS settings.
  • Process Inventory: One row per running process on this machine: PID and parent, threads and working set, the executable path and the command line.
  • Named Pipes: Every named pipe on this machine by name with its instance counts; Veeam's, SQL Server's and PostgreSQL's marked with their service. No pipe is opened.

Installed software

  • Installer Cache Check: The installed products by UpgradeCode or name, the cached package Windows keeps for each and whether it is there, and an installer or ISO folder checked against them.

The quick checks open in their own windows, from this page or by their keys anywhere in SAT.

Process Inventory

Process Inventory lists every process running on this machine, one row each: PID and parent, threads, working set, the executable path and the command line.

Before You Begin

  • Run SAT as administrator to read every process's path and command line. Without it, WMI often gives none for system processes and for other accounts' processes.
  • Run SAT as root to read other accounts' executables. Without it they read path not readable.
To list the running processes, do the following:

  2. Choose Inventory. The table lists each process with its PID and parent, threads, working set, executable and command line.
  3. Type in Filter rows to narrow the list, and select a row to read it in full.

Tools > Host Diagnostics > Time Check (F7)

Time Check (F7)

This machine's clock against its time source: the time zone, the configured source, and the difference one query to that source reads. Kerberos refuses sign-ins past a 5 minute difference. The converter reads a time from a log in the zone the log was written in.

  • Clock. Press Check to ask the configured source, or type a time server first to ask that one.
  • From a log. Paste a timestamp, or its whole line, into Timestamp from a log, choose the log with Log... or drop the log on the window, and press Convert. The offset comes from the log's own header (its UTC time or UTC offset) or the zone it names.
  • Written in. For a log without its own clock, choose the zone it was written in, or type a UTC offset.
  • Show in. The same moment in another zone, such as another machine's, to find the matching lines in that machine's logs.
The converter reads Veeam log line prefixes, Unix time, .NET ticks and Windows FILETIME values. A zone from the list applies its own daylight saving dates for the date read; a typed offset is used as it is.

Command line: time check and time convert.

To compare this machine's clock with its time source, do the following:
  1. Press F7.
  2. Press Check to ask the configured source, or type a time server first to ask that one.
  3. Read the time zone, the configured source and the difference. Kerberos refuses sign-ins past a 5 minute difference.
To convert a time from a log, do the following:
  1. Paste a timestamp, or its whole line, into Timestamp from a log.
  2. Choose the log with Log..., or drop the log on the window.
  3. For a log without its own clock, choose the zone it was written in, or type a UTC offset.
  4. Press Convert. Show in gives the same moment in another zone.

Volume Check (F9)

Every volume on this machine and what it sits on: an internal disk with its controller and driver, a USB drive, an iSCSI or Fibre Channel LUN, or an SMB or NFS share. With each: the file system, free space, compression and encryption, and on ReFS and XFS whether Veeam's Fast Clone can work there.

Tools > Host Diagnostics > Service and Process Watch (F12)

Service and Process Watch (F12)

Veeam's services and processes with the ports each one listens on, read again every 2 seconds while it watches, so what starts, ends or restarts during a job shows as it happens.

  • Watch. Leave veeam in Names that hold, or type another part of a name, and press Start watching. Then start or retry the job.
  • Changes. Each start, end or restart appears in the list below with its time. Add to #note keeps the list with the case.
  • Its log. Choose a process or service that ended or restarted and press Its log. It lists the Veeam logs written in the 2 minutes before the change was seen, newest first; the one chosen opens in SAT's viewer at the line written before then.
  • Its ports. Opens the Local Port Checker on the selected process.
Veeam names its logs by job, task and service, so Its log shows every log written at that time.

Command line: watch.

To watch Veeam's services and processes during a job, do the following:
  1. Press F12.
  2. Leave veeam in Names that hold, or type another part of a name.
  3. Press Start watching, then start or retry the job.
  4. Read each start, end or restart in the list below with its time.
  5. Choose a process or service that ended or restarted and press Its log to open the Veeam logs written in the 2 minutes before the change, or Its ports to open the Local Port Checker on it.
  6. Press Add to #note to keep the list with the case.
